Ministers are waking up to Britain’s gas supply risks. It’s time for decisions

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:30:47 GMT

Despite declining consumption, the country will still need lots of gas in coming years but solutions aren’t forthcoming

UK risks running out of gas by 2030s, ministers told

The penny is dropping in government. Britain, even in rapid energy transition mode, will still need a lot of gas in the years ahead – and needs to know how the gas will arrive.

It could hardly be otherwise when there are 24m households with a gas connection, largely for heating, and the pace of heat pumps adoption is miserable. Last year gas comprised about a third of the UK’s overall energy needs. Though annual consumption is in decline, the days of peak use during a bleak midwinter can still be as high as ever.

The difficulty has been getting ministers to focus on the combination of declining North Sea volumes (about 40% of supply), skimpy levels of gas storage and limited capacity for importing the stuff via tanker. Until now, the default position under successive governments has been that the market will provide.

A scary report from the energy system operator last November, however, warned of “an emerging risk” to gas supplies at the turn of the decade if an important piece of infrastructure, such as one of only three terminals for importing liquefied natural gas (LNG), were to be offline during a cold snap. Now comes the government’s formal response.

Or, rather, it’s half a response since this was an interim version cloaked in the language of “more analysis needed”. But one significant shift was reasonably clear: the government thinks it will probably have to intervene to ensure sufficient gas capacity and infrastructure is in place. That could mean contracts to underpin more storage, more import terminals or something else.

There are three observations to make about this report. First, ministers need to hurry up and decide what they want, as opposed to repeatedly describing the menu of options. “We have a responsibility to the millions of households that will be heated by gas for years ahead, the industries that rely on it for essential production and the power system in which gas continues to play a key role,” declared energy minister Michael Shanks. What he did not do, however, was set out a timetable for choosing what kit is needed and by when.

If, for example, regeneration of Centrica’s Rough storage site off the coast of Yorkshire is one solution, that £2bn project won’t happen overnight. Nor could alternative onshore or offshore storage facilities, or even floating offshore import terminals, be summoned immediately. If the 2030 risk of running short of gas is real, get on with it.

Second, what about this winter? That challenge wasn’t mentioned. “Swift and decisive action is also required to address potential near-term challenges,” said Jon Butterworth, chief executive of National Gas, which runs the gas network, back in February. While he added that “work is already well under way,” it is hard to find anybody who can describe what has been done in response to the disruption to global LNG supplies.

Centrica has not been injecting gas into Rough this year because it can’t make the finances stack up, meaning Britain will enter winter with even less storage than usual. In the meantime, continental European storage, which Britain normally taps via interconnectors during the cold months, is projected to be lower than average for Hormuz-related reasons. And wholesale gas prices are rising, amid anticipated global competition for LNG cargoes.

Third, Tuesday’s report was not about North Sea policy, but represented another reason to approve the Jackdaw gasfield. It would, after all, be bizarre to outline a potential supply crunch that has been caused, in large part, by growing reliance on imports, and then disallow a field that will make the problem slightly smaller. Jackdaw will account for about 6% of domestic North Sea gas volumes and could be up and running in time for winter. Whatever the awkward “optics”, there is another decision to make soon.

Charity campaigner who died after microlight crash was filming Apple TV series, inquest hears

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:18:11 GMT

Claire Lomas was filming content for project promoting tech company’s Vision Pro headset in Jordan, hearing told

A disability campaigner who was paralysed from the chest down died after her microlight crashed while filming a TV series for Apple, an inquest has heard.

Claire Lomas, 44, who was the first person to complete a marathon with the help of a “bionic” suit, died five weeks after the adapted aircraft she was travelling in “veered off the runway” and hit a large rock while landing in Amman, Jordan.

The mother of two had become a noted campaigner for disability charities after a horse riding accident in 2007 left her paralysed.

Louise Pinder, senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, told the inquest on Tuesday that Lomas suffered multiple severe traumatic injuries during the crash on 15 July and was taken to King Hussein medical centre, where she died on 22 August.

The hearing, which took place at County Hall in Glenfield, Leicester, heard that at the time of her accident, Lomas had been wearing an Apple Vision Pro headset and was in the process of filming content for the tech company to be used in a series promoting the product.

Lina Zilinskaite, a senior producer for Atlantic Productions, told the inquest that Apple had commissioned her company to create the series, and Lomas was one of several athletes selected to perform “some sort of challenge or feat” in different episodes.

Zilinskaite told the court that Lomas had been “very enthusiastic and keen and excited about the opportunity” and that she had obtained a licence to fly a microlight, the small aircraft she was piloting at the time of the crash, years before the series was commissioned.

This was supported by Ben Ashman, a microlight designer and manufacturer, who said that Lomas had bought her own version of the aircraft between 2022 and 2023, which had been adapted to support her inability to use her feet.

Speaking on the events leading up to the crash, Zilinskaite told the hearing that Lomas’ flight had been scheduled for the day before but was cancelled “because of strong winds”. Zilinskaite also said that there had been test flights using the Vision Pro in the UK without Lomas, and that she had flown the microlight herself before the accident, albeit without wearing the headset.

On the day of the flight, the inquest was told that Lomas had taken off from the runway in Jordan without issue and remained in the air for roughly 15 minutes before attempting to land, but that upon descending her “approach was not quite straight on” and that she “veered off the runway” before striking a large rock.

The inquest heard that Lomas, who had completed the London Marathon over the course of 17 days in 2012 with the assistance of “bionic” legs, had been “excited” to return to the UK after the crash and see her family, but that her health rapidly deteriorated after catching an infection which led to her death.

Pinder said Lomas’ family had raised concerns about the quality of care in the Jordanian hospital, but that it was not within her jurisdiction to investigate that formally.

The inquest continues.

Andy Burnham should resist populist pressure on jail sentences

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:05:40 GMT

Nik Wood says the prime minister must be tough on the causes of crime, Henry Rossi calls for him to resolve the IPP crisis, while Janet Carter considers victims of domestic abuse

As you say in your editorial (The Guardian view on early prisoner release: don’t lose sight of systemic reform, 12 August), governments of all stripes have bowed to pressure for ever longer sentencing. For instance, the killers of PC Andrew Harper would now face mandatory life sentences, campaigned for across the board. It was the unlikely figure of Douglas Hurd, the Conservative home secretary, who said that prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse. That expense is always one that is tempting for governments demonstratively to minimise.

The result is a prison service that hasn’t got room for all those the courts convict, nor enough staff or scope to reform and rehabilitate them for the benefit of society. The assault that has been made on Parole Board and probation decision-making and capabilities compounds this.

So, Andy Burnham has inherited a decision that has nothing to do with judicially assessed sentencing and remission, merely to do with patching a hole in the balance sheet. If he does indeed want to avoid a repeat of this shambles, as you report, then he has to grow a backbone and stand up against the populist pressures to appear “tough on crime”, and find the money to be “tough on the causes of crime”. Nik WoodLondon

The government’s scramble to keep PC Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars while freeing up space in prisons is the latest example of UK policy shortcomings and a subsequent failure to remedy the scandal. None stand out more than the unaddressed injustice of imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences. Abolished over a decade ago and described as “psychological torture” by the UN, over 2,000 people remain trapped in prisons on IPP sentences.

Andy Burnham has pledged to find an early resolution to the IPP crisis, but too often politicians have decried scandals, only to then kick the can down the road.

Resolving IPP would end one of the greatest scandals in our criminal justice system and also ease the burden on our creaking prisons – resentencing IPP prisoners could free up the equivalent of four prisons. The time for acknowledging injustices and promising to conduct a review is over. It’s time to act. Henry RossiBristol

With reference to your article (More women will die if domestic abusers leave prison early, victim’s parents warn, 17 August), there is an effective way for the government to mitigate this sad fact. This is to legislate to ensure that the court must always consider future protection in all cases of domestic abuse, rather than just focus on immediate incarceration.

How? To make it a presumption that the relevant “add-on” ancillary order is always considered whenever available, or give reasons why the order is not appropriate. For instance, it may be disproportionate given the facts of the case, or the victim may give freely held views that they genuinely do not want an order to be made.

For instance, an add-on restraining order with terms to exclude the perpetrator from the home and work areas of the victim, for life, so that the victim has some security and safety whenever the release date happens to fall. Various protective orders are available, but they are not yet an obligatory consideration in open court. They should be, along with obligatory victim consultation before sentence. Janet CarterRetired barrister, Leeds

Contemplating death helps us to really value life

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:05:36 GMT

Say the thing, mend the relationship, share the story – and then get on with living, says end-of-life doula Rebecca Jo-Rushdy, while Jane Andrew thinks EM Forster said it best

What struck me most about this article (What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work, 13 August) is the idea that preparing for the end of life can actually help us live more fully now.

As an end-of-life doula, I have seen how a terminal diagnosis can suddenly bring clarity. The things that once felt urgent often fall away, while relationships, memories, unfinished conversations and the question of what we leave behind become profoundly important. But I don’t believe that we should have to wait for a diagnosis to begin that work.

We often think of “getting our affairs in order” as something practical: writing a will, sorting passwords or deciding what happens to our possessions. Yet there is something much more human underneath all of this. It is about asking: what matters to me? What do I want my family to know? What stories, photographs, objects or values do I want to pass on? And, perhaps most importantly, what can I let go of so that the people I love are not left carrying unnecessary burdens?

I have come to see this as creating a joyful legacy. Decluttering, when approached this way, isn’t simply about having a tidier home. It can be a way of making space for the life we are actually living – while making things a little easier for those who may one day have to sort through what we leave behind.

The article rightly reminds us that none of us knows how much time we have. Perhaps the most loving response to that uncertainty is not to fear death, but to use its inevitability as an invitation: say the thing, mend the relationship, celebrate the birthday, sort the photographs, share the story – and then get on with living. Rebecca Jo-RushdyEdinburgh

I recently recovered from major cancer surgery, and Sarah Phillips’ article rang very true. Being forced to embrace my own mortality has helped me find what truly shines in ordinary life. EM Forster put it so well: “Death destroys a man: the idea of Death saves him”. Jane AndrewPerth

Poverty and weariness in Nigel Farage’s Clacton

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:05:31 GMT

Vanessa Scanlan says the constituency is desperately in need of a decent MP who would offer genuine support for the problems it faces. Plus letters from Leila Roberts and Richard Ellis

I live in the Clacton constituency, in one of the surrounding villages, some distance from the town, and I agree with Sarah Elizabeth Cox’s characterisation of the town (Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here, 12 August).

When I go to Clacton to take my kids to the beach or to the cinema, there is a sudden shift in the character of the area. The deprivation radiates in some streets. It is painful to see the residents so keenly in need of a decent MP to offer genuine support for a town with so many problems being exploited by Nigel Farage.

I have worked my way through a number of podcasts and news articles during this byelection and the 2024 general election campaigns. Those cherrypicked vox pops and even the broader and more balanced reporting speak of poverty and weariness in the Clacton population. Is it any wonder that a charismatic man offering a simple answer to complex problems is held on to so tightly?Vanessa Scanlan Great Bentley, Essex

So Nigel Farage couldn’t attend his election results because of security concerns – despite the £5m he was given for his security. Blimey, Clacton must be dangerous. Leila RobertsRipon, North Yorkshire

The Clacton byelection’s rash of joke candidates has been pretty much passed off by every media outlet as just another example of the “British sense of humour”, originating more or less from the frivolous establishment of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 1982. However, I am sufficiently old enough to recall that amid the laughter, anxious voices warned then that this could also fuel a debasement of the serious importance of politics and government in the UK. A case can be made that the far right’s rise in the UK has been partly fuelled by the way that politics has been reduced to a joke by such allegedly harmless shenanigans, which in fact implicitly or openly rely on reducing mainstream politics to the status of uniformly useless – “they are all the same”. Richard EllisDerby

Autonomous drones and the future of war in an AI-driven world

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 17:05:27 GMT

Machines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe, writes military surgeon Dr Darren Mann

Stuart Russell is right that AI’s builders fear losing control of it (Experts are warning: our AI arms race is putting humanity at risk, 11 August). But it is not only a future superintelligence’s problem; it is already loaded into weapons, where a loss of control kills a civilian today, not humanity tomorrow.

An autonomous drone told to clear a “kill box” is the genie your other columnists described (How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement, 18 July): it does what it is told, killing whatever is inside, combatant or child. The gap between a target and a lawful target is the principle of distinction, which no instruction closes, because the instruction was lawful.

Russell doubts asking a superintelligence how to control itself. In war the check need not be another opaque mind but a deterministic one: its rulebook the Geneva conventions, its judgments auditable, returned to a human. We need not trust it; we can check it. Some of us are working on it.

A further danger is peculiar to war. Autonomy is sold as combat without our own dead, and a bloodless war is easier to start. But that is a fallacy: you can take the human from the targeting loop, not the nation from the war. Ground must be won and held; the dead still come, in attack or defence. Armies no longer go to war; nations do.

If we cannot teach a drone to keep the laws of war, we will not teach a greater intelligence to keep faith with all we value. To abandon those laws for survival is the confusion of interests with values that our strategists warn against; here the two are one. Machines that kill without distinction, answerable to no one, leave no one safe. Our interests do not merely permit us to hold the line; they demand it. Dr Darren MannMilitary surgeon, London

‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringe

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 16:25:40 GMT

How do you keep audiences gripped while cycling 27km per show? From the Australian recreating a Tour de France win to a ‘toxically positive’ spin queen, we meet the acts bringing Olympian fitness to Edinburgh

Blood and sweat drip to the floor. Tears are on their way. In a small room in Edinburgh, Megan Tomei is cleat-clipped into a stationary bike, yelling above the music as she leads a high-intensity spin class gone wrong. “We take the thing you’re running from,” Tomei shouts, pink lights bouncing off her gleaming shoulders, “and turn it into fuel!” This is SpinQueen™, one of a handful of shows at this year’s fringe demanding epic endurance from their performers through the use of jazzed-up gym equipment. Employing various bikes and a treadmill to authentically illustrate the struggle for success, the pain of failure, and the escape from reality, a profoundly fit group of actors are pushing themselves to their physical limits.

Across the city, Connor Delves’s calves are worth watching. The workout from his cycling-obsessed play, Cadel: Lungs on Legs, is so powerful that people have come up to him after, wanting to touch them. “To make sure they’re real,” says Delves, who cycles a whopping 27km per show. Does he mind this attention? He shrugs. “If they’re OK with getting their hands sweaty, go for it.”

Delves grew up in his parents’ bike shop in Perth, Western Australia. His mum was a triathlete, his dad an international mountain-biker. “It’s always been acting and sport for me,” he says. When he was replaced by a bigger name in a transferring show, he decided to make a production in which he was irreplaceable. “I’d never seen a play that showed endurance sport at its best,” he says, “where the sport is an actual effort.”

In 2016, Baby Reindeer’s Richard Gadd won the Edinburgh comedy award for Monkey See Monkey Do, an exposing show about toxic masculinity and sexual assault, performed on a treadmill. Two decades before, performance artist Kim Noble pounded away on a treadmill while the other half of their double act, Stuart Silver, played chess against the audience. Over lockdown, Katie Mitchell created eco-theatre show A Play for the Living in a Time of Extinction, with cyclists generating the show’s lights and sound. But few shows that involve this kind of equipment are about sport, where the exercise is in the story as well as in the doing.

With Cadel, this is what Delves set out to do. The result is a sincere, leg-burning ode to Cadel Evans, the first Aussie to win the Tour de France. Delves performs on a series of the real bikes that Evans used to win the 2011 race, clamped in place. The operation is a family affair: Delves’s father is the show’s mechanic. Head down, Delves’s teardrop-shaped helmet is steady as his legs whir round for the sprint stages. Remarkably riding the same mountain gradients as they do in the Tour, Delves is adept at explaining clearly to the uninitiated how the race works. It’s evident just how tough it is: every stage, every day, every kilometre. “It means you’ve got to think about nutrition,” Delves says of his show. “About sleep.” He quit drinking to train for it. “It means treating acting like being an athlete.”

While Evans’s story is the hero’s arc, The Distance is about the also-rans. “I’m interested in what happens to the legions of sportspeople who are very, very good, but not good enough to make a living from it,” says Ben Norris, the show’s writer and performer, and vocally recognisable as farmer’s son Ben in The Archers. “For every one who wins the Olympics,” he says, “there are at least eight who lose the final. Then 100 or 200 who were in the heats. Then tens of thousands who are very good but don’t get there.” So, he asks, what happens then? “Who are you when the thing to which your identity has been shackled is no longer viable?”

Norris plays Chris, a young boy realising his potential as a cross-country runner and dreaming of competing in the Olympics. The Distance is inspired by Norris’s time as a teenage international long-distance runner, but he worked hard to extricate it from himself. When he was mentored by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, she told him: “Be less concerned with being likable.” During each show, he runs roughly 8km on a “geriatric, old, foldable treadmill” that he’s wheeled all over the country. “One time, a local MP helped me on to the train with it,” he says. In Edinburgh, on Summerhall’s main stage, the treadmill is surrounded by a scaffolding pole, which Norris nimbly clambers over as Chris’s success rises and rises – and then begins to fall.

Norris starts running as the audience file into the room. Soon, his clothes are drenched. As he strips down, we see the effort this is taking; his chest heaving, his body glistening. The sweat and ragged breath are important, he explains. “You’re watching it cost something. You’re watching this body really work.” That cost is already making itself evident. Norris pulled his calf in March, then again in April. “I’ve had to start behaving like I’m an elite athlete again, in terms of the rigour of my training and recovery,” he says. “I’m not 18 any more. Everything takes longer on an older body.”

To be fit enough for the show, he has been cross-training, doing strength and conditioning, and phoning friends while on the treadmill to practise speaking at the same time as running at a furious speed. Throughout the fringe, he’s forcing himself to rest. “I’ve done a musical at the fringe and that requires a different kind of discipline. This will be like that, but on steroids.” He frowns. “Although crucially,” he says, “not on steroids.” His one request for accommodation: could he please have a bath?

I want to get a sense of the effort demanded by these shows, so when I talk to Tomei, the creator and performer of SpinQueen™, before the fringe, I suggest we do it on exercise bikes. My thighs soon regret it. “Oh God,” says Tomei, halfway through our chat. “I’m sweating so much.” She is in New York, calling from the spin studio at which she works. I quickly realise how hard it is to speak and ride at the same time.

In SpinQueen™, Tomei plays a heightened, emotionally cracked version of herself as our manic spin instructor, spewing out “toxic positivity” as Tomei calls it, her character obsessed with thinness, optimisation and escape from the quiet that lets thoughts seep in. “Keep pushing, keep starving!” she calls in the show with a too-wide grin. In real life, Tomei is similarly peppy, but without the desperate about-to-fall-apart energy of her character. But that version of herself isn’t a world away, she says; the story’s climax borrows from a traumatic experience she had with an ex. When our narrator won’t allow herself to stop cycling, Tomei says: “It’s a physical representation of her emotional state.”

Sweat is blurring my vision now. “Oh God, no, same,” Tomei tries to reassure me. Every show, she cycles 16km, wanting people to feel the pain her character goes through, emotionally and physically. Tomei started taking spin classes with her dad in high school, and began teaching it as a way to earn money alongside acting. But after running the New York marathon, she got injured. “I had to slow down for the first time in my life,” she says. “I struggled with it, and it made me think of all the standards we hold ourselves to, because of what we think makes us better or successful. It made me think: ‘Why are we killing ourselves trying to reach this standard that can’t be met?’”

What happens if these performers fall or twist an ankle during the fringe? “The same thing as in the Tour de France,” Delves says frankly. “I think that’s part of the allure of this. There’s no understudy.” With her massage gun packed, Tomei is more conscious of the emotional health she needs to maintain across the festival. “Every performance, I’m reliving what happened to me,” she says. “It’s a high-intensity emotional workout too.”

Even when their characters near the dreamed-of success in these shows, failure is only a breath away. One fall, one second behind in a race, one last chance. These plays capture the itch of pushing just that tiny bit harder, as well as the dangers of running on empty. “There’s a little ambition monster within you,” Norris says, “that will wonder if you should just quit everything else and give this one last big go.” You can keep batting it down, he says, but the monster is persistent. “LA Olympics 2028?” Norris muses, only just joking. “Is it too late?”

SpinQueen™ is at Jade Studio at Greenside @ George Street, until 29 August. The Distance, Main Hall at Summerhall, until 31 August. Cadel: Lungs on Legs, Auditorium at Gilded Balloon at the Museum, until 30 August; then Riverside Studios, London, 13 October-15 November

The ‘big-ass bag’ – do you really need a tote you can carry a small human in?

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 16:12:19 GMT

Lululemon’s absurdly capacious 80-litre bag will set you back a small fortune – and it’s one of the cheapest giant holdalls on the market

Name: Big-Ass Bags.

Age: The titular “Big-Ass Bag” launched this month (but large carrying receptacles have been available for centuries).

Appearance: Big ass.

Hey, who are you calling big ass? An absurdly capacious Luluemon tote.

How big is it really? Oh, it’s enormous-ass: 80 litres.

I don’t understand why bags are measured in litres – what am I going to do, fill it with milk? People on TikTok are managing to fill it with themselves.

OK, that is pretty big-ass. People are loving mocking its ludicrous dimensions online: “I know a studio apartment when I see one,” an Instagram commenter said. Product reviews include: “I took it with me to my summer backpacking trip. I was able to bring back the Eiffel Tower, coliseum [sic] and many other monuments.” Others have joked that it “runs small”: “I can only fit two of my five kids in this bag,” someone complained.

Does it have any genuine fans? Refinery 29 claims it’s a “brilliant solution for lugging everything at once”.

Are other big-ass bags available? Yes, they’re extremely on trend. There’s Loewe’s Puzzle Fold XL, The Row’s Marlo 14, or the cavernous Chanel beach bag Dua Lipa was recently seen carrying. That’s the one Women’s Wear Daily said back in April signalled “a return to dramatically oversized bags”.

Dramatically oversized is right. Bet it’s dramatically pricey too. The Chanel one will cost about £6,000 ($8,000).

That’s the price of a car! But what price a bag you could actually put a car into? Lululemon’s bag is a more reasonable £228.

Alternatively, I could plump for one of those zip-up plastic laundry bags – six for a tenner at Tesco. Also très chic! Balenciaga did a high-fashion version in 2016 (for £975).

Wasn’t “high fashion” trying to get us excited about absurdly tiny handbags five minutes ago? It needs to make its mind up. Yes, nano-bags have had their moments – you might recall seeing Lizzo carrying a Valentino one big enough for a single piece of chewing gum at the American Music Awards in 2019. And now you mention it, US Vogue actually said in April we “need a Teeny-Tiny Tote this Summer”.

What? Fashion can’t have it both ways! Argh, I’m ditching bags altogether. Sorry, I can’t let you do that – abandoning handbags and holding all your stuff in a claw grip was briefly a thing last year, but that’s ancient history.

Do say: “I like big bags and I cannot lie.”

Don’t say: “That was no solar eclipse, it was a Lululemon Big-Ass Bag.”

I’m 50 years old. Why do I still struggle with the need to be liked?

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 16:00:49 GMT

An over-investment in people-pleasing can be emotionally costly. Here’s how I’m training myself to be OK with letting people down

A few months ago, my 10-year-old daughter and I went to our neighborhood cafe. At the counter, the owner greeted us with her typical effusion of warmth and welcome. Instead of greeting her in kind, my daughter looked on with a stony expression and ungiving eyes.

My face flushed. I was embarrassed and incensed by what I perceived as blatant rudeness. You could at least smile, I thought.

When we left, I pulled my daughter aside and gave her a firm talk about respect and manners, but her face dropped and she looked like she might cry. I quickly realized that she was in a bad mood, and totally unaware of her external affect. I felt bad for not approaching the conversation differently – I had assumed she recognized her impoliteness, that she was taking a stab at playing “sulky irreverent teen”.

That’s when it hit me: by dictating that she should comport herself contrary to how she was actually feeling, I was reinforcing society’s attempts to mold girls and women into automatons who reflexively try to please everyone but themselves. It’s ironic, because I had written an entire book to warn her about doing just that: Ugly: A Letter to My Daughter. I knew these types of messages often lead to what psychologist Mary Pipher writes about in Reviving Ophelia: a “split self” that often results in the creation of a “false self” in line with gendered expectations.

Psychologists and studies indicate that an over-investment in people-pleasing and the quest to appear “nice” are emotionally costly. They amplify stress, impede individual fulfillment and self-actualization, and can lead to self-alienation.

I had to ask myself: isn’t my daughter entitled to be in a bad mood? To not mirror someone else’s happy disposition? Why should she fake a smile or express enthusiasm she doesn’t feel? Surely being raised to participate in these gendered theatrics is where the “split” Pipher talks about begins.

Don’t get me wrong – I don’t think manners are trivial. Smiling, holding the door, greeting people and expressing gratitude nurture mutual respect and affection between friends and strangers alike. But a lesson in politeness can so easily tip into encouraging servility in girls.

I’ve spent most of my life people-pleasing. It wasn’t until the last few years of my 40s that I started resisting that urge.

But before then, how often had I violated my own feelings, boundaries and wishes to ensure I was likable? How often had I said “yes” to plans I didn’t really want to partake in or echoed a sentiment I didn’t entirely agree with?

My deep – nearly existential – desire to be likable came, in part, from feeling abnormal and believing I could hide my queerness with 24/7 agreeability. Concealing my lesbianism in situations that felt unwelcome – or worse, unsafe – I’d adopted the affectations of femininity in various ways. As long as I remained feminine in my extreme likability, I could offset the internal and external cultural messaging that lesbians are angry, ugly freaks. But nothing made me realize the extent to which I wanted to be liked as when I started substitute teaching at public schools in New York City at the age of 48.

The first time I stood in front of a classroom buzzing with unimpressed kids, I desperately, stupidly, pathetically wanted them to like me. I felt like an awkward teenage girl again, trying to adapt to 10-year-old notions of cool. I softened my voice and overworked the muscles in my face to evince a perma-smile, even when students were being loud, disruptive and disrespectful.

I felt angry, but knew better than to yield to a displeasing scowl or a voice tinged with fury.

As feminist journalist Rebecca Traister put it in her brilliant book, Good and Mad: The Revolutionary Power of Women’s Anger: “Women’s anger will be – as it has long been – cast as ugly, unappealing, dangerous, something to be shut down or jeered. Nothing, we have long been assured, is more unattractive in a woman than anger.”

Think of all the language used to describe – or rather, dismiss – an irritated or furious woman. She’s difficult, aggressive, challenging, crazy, a witch, a bitch, a Medusa, a hellcat. Her “upset” is pathologized – and it’s enough to make any woman reach for the social ease of likability.

For me, as a queer person whose gender isn’t fully aligned with traditional femininity, I felt that expressing my anger would only amplify my aesthetic inadequacies. Being cheerful was a way to soften my less conventional presentation and manner – to sidestep the “angry lesbian” trope and the ugliness other people ascribe to it.

Furious outbursts and chronic expressions of anger are never acceptable in a classroom, but neither is quietly enduring inappropriate behavior. The days of stiff smiles and a voice dripping with syrup began grating on me. I didn’t want to tacitly teach children that misbehavior and disrespect would be greeted with a silent, acquiescent smile. I needed to get comfortable with my authority and their displeasure, fast.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

I started watching seasoned teachers manage their classrooms and I noticed the most effective educators followed four core practices: they give clear directives about what behavior is and is not acceptable at the outset and throughout the school year. They address transgressors immediately after they have defied a classroom rule, every single time. They balance discipline with affection and encouragement. Finally, they are not punitive.

In return, they earned more than likability – they earned students’ respect and trust. I adopted these practices and even started applying them to my life outside the classroom.

As I’ve gained more experience, turned 50 and experienced the many daily assaults of perimenopause, I’ve grown less patient and less concerned with popular opinion. These days, I raise my voice, clarify my boundaries and express discontent with insolence.

Now, instead of going along with what other people say, I’m more assertive. “Thanks for inviting me, but I feel like nesting today,” I might respond during an exhausting week. Or, to friends who pick restaurants closer to their neighborhood than mine, I might redirect: “Hey, can we meet somewhere in the middle?”

The likability norm still has its hold on me. But what’s really helped me get comfortable with the discomfort of not people-pleasing is wanting to model for my daughter the OK-ness of disappointing others or setting them straight. And I’ve started to see her do the same: she told a boy who liked her that she only wanted to be friends. At a slumber party, she took out a book while her friends played Roblox. On a family vacation, her cousin wanted to play inside, but she wanted to go to the beach – so she went by herself.

It’s not easy to disappoint people or go it alone, especially in the face of resistance; women often face gaslighting, retaliation, even violence when they refuse to accept mistreatment. In those moments, do I feel like the strands of my hair have transformed into snakes and that I’ve just sprouted a face full of warts? Yes. Do I care? Less and less, especially when I see my male colleagues, with their broad shoulders and deep voices, command attention and respect to a degree I’m denied. This is, of course, a symptom of a sexist culture – one we have no hope of changing until we stop over-prioritizing everyone else’s pleasure and comfort above our own.

And ultimately, I don’t care how people respond to my assertiveness. What matters to me is that I’m demarcating my limits, which is critical to my own dignity and self-respect. But dropping the mask of accommodation and self-denial doesn’t just affect the individual. The more we all do it, the more it feels OK to express our full humanity – our likability and our disagreeability, our beauty and our ugliness.

Stephanie Fairyington is a writer in New York City who just published her first book, Ugly: A Letter to My Daughter

Grenfell cladding firm Arconic paid shareholders £23m more in compensation than to fire victims

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 15:47:19 GMT

Report’s author said findings highlighted ‘near-total failure’ to hold corporations accountable over the disaster that killed 72 people

The company behind Grenfell Tower’s flammable cladding gave more compensation to its shareholders than to victims of the disaster, an investigation has found.

Arconic, which made and sold the cladding panels found to be the “primary cause” of the rapid spread of the Grenfell fire, paid $74m (£54.7m)) to its shareholders for economic loss they incurred after the blaze.

In contrast, the company paid $43m (£31.8m) to the estates of the fire’s victims and survivors after a lengthy legal battle. Across both payouts, all but $2m was covered by Arconic’s insurers.

The findings are part of a new report by thinktank Common Wealth and financial investigations group FIND, which calls for stronger corporate accountability laws in England and Wales to ensure future misconduct does not go “unpunished and undeterred”.

“Arconic successfully avoided consequential accountability for its role in the fire through a series of ordinary business practices,” the report said.

Grenfell United, which represents the bereaved and survivors of the fire, said the investigation showed how “corporate structures and legal systems have allowed those responsible to move on while our community continues to live with the consequences”.

“Grenfell was not just a tragedy – it was a preventable disaster. We hope these findings help drive the legal and political changes needed to ensure no company can evade responsibility in this way again,” they said.

A total of 72 people, including 18 children, died as a result of the fire in the 24-storey Grenfell Tower in June 2017.

Arconic sold Reynobond PE, the flammable aluminium composite material (ACM) used to clad the tower. The inquiry into the blaze found the company “deliberately and dishonestly concealed from the market” the true danger of the product in the form in which it was used on Grenfell.

Arconic has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and a criminal investigation by the Metropolitan police has yet to bring charges against any individuals or companies in relation to the fire.

The report revealed how the Reynobond PE used on the tower made up less than 1% of annual Reynobond sales at the time, and said there was no evidence Arconic has tried to trace the rest of the product it has sold.

It had been selling Reynobond globally for at least 20 years before the Grenfell fire, and previously said it had sold 12.75m square metres of it in total.

The report urged Arconic to publicly reveal where the rest of the material had been sold, and said it should be debarred from public contracts in England until it does so.

after newsletter promotion

Common Wealth researcher and the report’s author, Leela Jadhav, said the findings “outline a near-total failure of legal mechanisms to hold corporations accountable”.

It also called for stronger laws in England to punish corporate misconduct, saying the country lags far behind other countries in doing this.

Its recommendations included making punitive damages available in England and Wales in cases where corporate illegality is implicated in death. Currently, these damages are awarded very rarely and only in narrowly defined circumstances.

Courts should be given the power to direct a portion of shareholder settlement recoveries to victim funds where third-party harm is identified, it said, and insurance companies should conduct human rights and environmental due diligence to ensure they do not “facilitate and encourage” misconduct.

The UK government has committed a maximum of £5.1bn to cladding removal, with £600m of public money put into an ACM Cladding Remediation Fund. The report said, “an order of punitive damages against Arconic could cover these expenses, at no public cost”.

Arconic declined to comment.

Things get even more tricky for Dicky Tice, the Reform deputy with lots of cash but zero self-awareness

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 15:35:11 GMT

Telling the country to enjoy the heat while it burns, you have to wonder if Tice has lost all sense of reality

These are the doggiest of dog days. Times when hours turn into days and almost nothing happens in between. Days of precious R&R, when only a few politicians venture out, and then only to fend off accusations they are doing next to nothing and prove they are still alive. Much like the rest of us. The silliest days of the silly season. Days that are made for men like Richard Tice.

There are some politicians who have the gift of sounding as if they know what they are talking about. There are those who you suspect are bullshitting but still give the benefit of the doubt. Then there are the ones you only have to look at to know they are completely clueless in every way. Never within the same postcode as plausibility. A walking miracle because somehow they have managed to persuade their party association and constituency voters that what they really need is someone who is visibly dim and incompetent. August gives us space to celebrate these men and women. None more so than Dicky. The apex male of stupidity. The idiot’s idiot.

It’s not clear if there has ever been much point to Dicky. Other than to encourage other halfwits that they can make half a name for themselves in public life providing they are blessed with plenty of cash and a total absence of self-awareness. Dicky likes to moan about diversity, equality and inclusion policies while remaining totally oblivious to the fact that were life to be a genuine meritocracy, he wouldn’t even make it to the starting line.

But that’s not to say Dicky doesn’t have his uses. A man with no idea of his own limitations could be just what Nigel Farage was looking for. The perfect beta supplicant who could be relied upon to do whatever he was told. Just as long as the instructions were crystal clear. There were no complaints from Dicky when just before the 2024 general election, Nige decided he was going to be Reform party leader after all.

Dicky knew his place. He smiled like the Mr Congeniality he hoped to be. Life was going quite well up until the Guardian revealed the £5m gift to Nige from Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Then the Sunday Times got in on the act with its reporting that if Farage became leader, Reform would repay or write off loans it received from Tice’s company in a deal presented by Farage and convicted fraudster George Cottrell. Things really began to fall apart.

The last few months haven’t been kind either to Reform or Dicky. One misstep after another. The party has been sliding in the polls, has called a byelection in Clacton which achieved little more than delaying an investigation by the parliamentary watchdog and handing 9,500 votes to a man with a bin on his head. As for Nige, he’s chosen to keep a much lower profile ever since he failed to come up with a plausible explanation for why he needed so much money. He didn’t even bother to attend the Clacton count, instead spending the night dancing with Dicky at Farage Fest.

All of which has made life tricky for Dicky. Reform have needed someone to step up and fill the vacuum left by Nige and the only one who has been consistently available has been Tice. And replacing one vacuum with another doesn’t really cut it. Their combative home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf has been sidelined, Lee Anderson has kept a low profile and the others don’t really count. Nige had high hopes for Robert Jenrick but Reform’s ratings plummet every time Honest Bob makes an appearance.

Which may be why Dicky was sent out with Honest Bob on Monday to try and dilute the animosity. Only it didn’t quite work out as Dicky rather stole Jenrick’s thunder. Because what people took away from Reform’s press conference wasn’t that Dicky would quite like benefits claimants to clean the high streets, it was that Dicky was thoroughly enjoying the extreme hot weather.

While the rest of the country was worried about drought and wildfires, and farmers were predicting armageddon, Dicky was having the time of his life. Forget the pint of beer that he has to drink when photographed with the riff-raff, Dicky was thrilled he would soon be able to neck vintage English fizzy wines that were better than champagne. When all things were considered, climate change was really just a state of mind. You could either get all doom and gloom about it. Or you could pretend it wasn’t really an issue, that attempts to combat it were a complete waste of time and try to make the most of it. We should all go out and have a barbecue. What was one more fire among so many?

Now try to imagine just how half-witted you have to be to actually say that. It’s bad enough thinking it. After all, we know that Kemi Badenoch appears to have much the same attitude as she plans to throw any Tories who believe in net zero targets out of the party. But even she knows better than to say any of this while there is a national emergency in place: however much it goes against her better judgment. But Dicky has no such qualms. Just says it as he sees it. Why worry about the state of the planet in 25 years time? As far as he is concerned all we have is today. Make hay while the sun shines. Only we can’t because the fields are burned.

So we are left with a conundrum. Were silly seasons always quite this silly? Does Dicky actually believe a word of what he says? Or has he infantilised himself so much by talking nonsense that he no longer knows what’s true. Or maybe he’s a secret agent, playing the long game to bring down Reform. The more you see of Dicky, the less there is.

Heavy rain on dry ground may cause UK floods but will not reverse drought

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 15:00:04 GMT

‘First meaningful rain for a long time’ is forecast but water firms continue to ask customers to restrict use

Floods and drought could hit the UK at the same time this week, with heavy rain forecast to fall on hard, parched soil.

While some parts of the UK will have the “first meaningful rain for a long time” in the coming days, it will not reverse widespread drought conditions that have put pressure on wildlife, farmers, firefighters and water resources.

On Tuesday, South East Water told customers in Kent to use water only for “essential” purposes, after taps ran dry on Monday for around 8,000 customers. Wessex Water imposed the UK’s latest hosepipe ban, covering 1.4m customers in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire.

The summer’s fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave will be followed by wetter and cooler weather that is much closer to the usual conditions for the time of the year, according to the Met Office.

Its deputy chief forecaster, Mike Silverstone, said showers were expected on Tuesday in the north of the country, particularly in the north-west, and that another area of rain would move into the south-west by the evening.

This would then probably spread east across the south, bringing the first spell of widespread rain to areas most in need. “Thursday will be a day of heavy showers across much of the UK. While some of these will be heavy, some areas will miss them altogether,” Silverstone said.

“As some of these showers could be intense, there is a chance of some surface water flooding as the rain falls on very dry and hard ground,” he added.

The forecast rain may bring some welcome relief to parched land and firefighters tackling wildfires, but water shortages will persist.

South East Water told customers in Kent on Tuesday that the levels in its storage tanks remained “critically low”, despite having restored supplies to 7,400 homes in Herne Bay, Rough Common and Blean on Tuesday. About 400 homes still had no water, the company’s spokesperson said.

A spokesperson from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the situation was “simply not good enough”.

“South East Water needs to go further and faster to reduce leaks and follow their drought plans to ensure supplies are not disrupted in even the driest of weather,” the spokesperson said.

South East Water was the first water company to issue a hosepipe ban this summer, on 3 July for customers in some parts of Kent. On Tuesday, Wessex Water became the latest, with its first ban since the summer of 1976.

The company blamed increased demand during the dry weather, but also longer-term weather forecasts that mean resources must be protected for customers and the environment.

On Friday, Environment Agency data showed five of England’s key reservoirs are currently “exceptionally low”, while the the National Hydrological Monitoring Programme warned low supplies were likely to persist into the autumn.

Thames Water also urged customers to continue to limit water use. The company said in an update on Tuesday that since it imposed its hosepipe ban on 23 July household demand had fallen by 3% across London and more than 6% across the Thames Valley and home counties.

July rainfall in the Thames catchment area was less than 1mm, which is 2% of the long-term average. Customers used about 100m litres more water a day than normal, putting pressure on rivers, reservoirs and the water network.

London reservoir storage is at 74% as a result, far lower than expected for this time of year.

Thames Water’s director of water, Martin Padley, said: “With reservoir levels below where we would expect them to be for this time of year and demand remaining high, we’re asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.

Liz Stephens, a professor in climate risk and resilience at the University of Reading, told PA Media it could take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.

“Here in the south-east, we’re still a month’s worth of rain below what we would normally expect by this point in the year, despite the heavy rainfall in January and February,” she said.

“As a result, while any rain which falls this week may help reduce the immediate wildfire risk, it will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and our rivers and reservoirs to return to normal. This means that we should expect hosepipe bans to be in place for some time.

“Floods can still occur during drought conditions and surface water flooding can even become more likely as baked soils are unable to soak up rainwater as quickly.”

Why is Sweden deporting Britons faster than any other EU country post-Brexit?

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 14:38:17 GMT

The official talk is of the government acting with understanding and flexibility. But devastated lives tell another story

There is anger about the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old retired nurse who has lived in Sweden for 21 years. Her husband died there; her son, grandchildren and home are there. Yet she has been told to leave because her post-Brexit residence application was late. Her case is appalling and predictable – but far from isolated.

The Guardian has also reported on the plight of Horace Mason, 74, who faces being deported after a court ruling, despite having lived in Sweden for 25 years. This is sad but not surprising.

When Sweden set out its plans in 2020, we at the Brits in Sweden campaign warned in an official submission that the application scheme could strip vulnerable people of their rights if they missed the deadline. We urged a flexible and generous approach, and later raised concerns about outreach and refusals with the UK government and European Commission. We have watched Britons fall off that cliff edge since 2021; only occasionally does a case reach the media.

The new scheme gave British residents safeguards under free-movement law – including assistance, reasonable grounds for lateness and proportionality – that were untested.

We were not alone. The Swedish Bar Association said the new rules must be applied generously to both evidence and deadlines, to which the government insisted that the authorities already had sufficient flexibility.

The truth of the situation is now clear, for the statistics only point in one direction. Almost 4,000 of 14,200 applications in Sweden have been refused. The UK Foreign Office calculates a 27.5% refusal rate – three times that of any other member state and far above the EU average of 3–4%. Eurostat records 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave Sweden since 2021, about a third of the EU total.

Reporting differences complicate detailed comparisons, but the statistics show a red flag consistent with lived experience. Kathleen Poole had advanced Alzheimer’s when Sweden tried to remove her in 2023. Nichola Stanlick arrived aged seven, 40 years ago, and applied on time, yet was refused withdrawal agreement protection and given a national permit expiring in 2027. Kenny Solomons, the husband of a Swedish singer, was forced to leave and would have to qualify under national law to return as a resident.

Data on genuine missed-deadline applications remains opaque. Earlier figures mixed them with legitimate later applicants, including people joining family members and those seeking permanent status. After we raised this with Whitehall, the UK challenged the data and Sweden no longer show it in EU reports. Among genuine missed-deadline cases brought to our 9,000-member group, we cannot verify one in which Sweden accepted the reasons for applying late.

The Brexit treaty called for an awareness campaign, but unlike Denmark and the Netherlands, the Swedish government chose not to contact registered Britons individually. Some people who enquired to Swedish authorities were told they need do nothing; official information did not always say that this meant “not yet”. Older people and those without computers were easily missed.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The then director general of the Swedish Migration Agency stated that he believed contacting registered Britons individually would not have made a difference. This is difficult to reconcile with the evidence base.

The problem is not confined to those who submitted late applications. Sweden sometimes refused withdrawal agreement status but granted temporary national permits. That merely kicks the can down the road. As those permits expire, some people cannot meet newer permanent-residence requirements, or no longer have the family circumstances on which their permits depended.

So why Sweden, and why now? The answer is that Sweden’s migration politics have moved sharply towards restriction. That cannot displace EU law, but it makes remedial action harder to defend politically. A Swedish faith in neutral rules and independent agencies can also mistake procedural uniformity for justice when radically different human circumstances are reduced to data points.

Britons in the EU are caught in a political perfect storm. EU citizens in Britain have a constituency and dedicated monitoring authority, whereas Britons are divided among 27 systems. Brexit created the problem, but did not require Sweden to conduct inadequate outreach, obscure statistics or stretch proportionality.

We are stuck in a very difficult middle: Brexiters resist admitting that Brexit created these problems, while some remainers resist criticising an EU member state. Both, in their relative positions, abandon the people the agreement protects.

In the Whitehall satire Yes, Prime Minister, the official response to a foreign problem progresses from “nothing is going to happen”, to “maybe we should do something about it, but there’s nothing we can do”, and finally to “maybe there was something we could have done, but it’s too late now”. The UK government and commission must intervene before reaching that final stage. Sweden should pause disputed removals, publish reliable cohort statistics and submit the scheme to independent review before more lives are irreversibly uprooted.

David Milstead is a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights campaigner, working through the Brits in Sweden group

Where on earth is Melania Trump?

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 14:32:47 GMT

In her husband’s first term, her absences sparked conspiracy theories. This time, she is somehow keeping an even lower profile

Anyone seen a 56-year-old woman around lately? Tall, cinnamon blond hair, fond of a fancy hat and, to quote Vogue, occasionally dresses like a “freelance magician”. She goes by the name “Melania Trump” or “first lady”, and she appears to be missing again. According to an analysis by the Daily Beast, Melania has only made 38 public appearances this year – with the last being the World Cup final. She’s been MIA for about a month.

To be fair, this isn’t out of character. During her first stint in the White House, the first lady’s frequent absences sparked various conspiracy theories, including one that she had a body double. But it seems Melania is keeping an even lower profile during Trump 2.0. NBC reported on Monday that she’s done about half as many public events as she did at this point in Trump’s first term. A senior adviser told the outlet she “prioritises results over appearances”. I dunno about that. Her highest-profile public appearance this year was when she held a surprise press conference telling everyone not to speculate about her relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. This had the predictable result of getting everyone to speculate about her relationship with the dead sex offender.

The first lady may be work-shy but she’s definitely not camera-shy. Melania starred in an eponymous documentary bankrolled by Amazon that hit theatres at the beginning of the year. Ted Hope, a former Amazon employee, told the New York Times that the $35m in promotion and $40m in rights meant it had to “be the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing”. He added: “How can it not be equated with currying favor or an outright bribe?” Jeff Bezos would vehemently deny such nasty smears. He has said that, while he had nothing to do with the project, it was a “good business decision”.

Good business or not, the Melania movie was not well received – the Guardian’s reviewer gave it zero stars. Nevertheless, it seems that more scintillating first lady content is on its way. A companion docuseries to the movie is coming to Prime Video this autumn. Earlier this month, one of Melania’s advisers told the conservative media network Real America’s Voice that this series will “open a little deeper into her career, as well as her philanthropy”. If her money-making schemes are anything to go by, Melania’s theory of philanthropy seems to be that charity begins at home.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘Even its loos are on the outside’: hi-tech, inside-out marvel the Lloyd’s building is partying with the public

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 14:21:16 GMT

It has been likened to a monster, an oil rig – and the Parthenon. Now, for its 40th birthday, the astonishing London landmark has joined the Open House festival, to grant admirers a rare look around the inside

In his 2012 book A New Kind of Bleak, the critic Owen Hatherley called it “monstrous, compelling” and utterly messed-up. Back in the 1980s, a then Prince Charles suggested it had been inspired by a North Sea oil rig. But none of this stopped it from becoming, in 2011, the youngest ever building to be given Grade I-listed status in the UK.

And now, as part of its 40th anniversary celebrations, the Lloyd’s building will open to the public for the first time since 2014 for one day only during London’s Open House festival. The iconic building in the heart of the financial district was designed by architect Richard Rogers to house the global insurance marketplace. Its futuristic facade has been a celebrated part of the City of London skyline since it opened in 1986, but the interior is rarely seen by the public. Visitor galleries with a view of the trading floor have long been shut for security reasons.

Open House festival is organised by the charity Open City, which aims to make architecture more accessible by inviting government offices, private properties and heritage buildings to let the public in. Free tickets for the Lloyd’s building are released tomorrow for the one day the building is open, on 19 September. The tour will include the underwriting room and the Adam Room as well as examining how the building was designed. “There was whooping in the office when the Lloyd’s building came in,” says festival director Celia Mead, “because we know our visitors really, really want to get inside this landmark institution.”

Lloyd’s is a key example of British hi-tech architecture. This late modernist style evolved in the 1970s and celebrates industrial engineering and prefabricated materials. Lloyd’s is famous for its exposed concrete frame and the six external steel towers that house its staircases, lifts, pipes and ducts. The building’s 12 glass lifts were the first of their kind in the UK, and each tower is permanently topped with steel cranes - partly for maintenance but also to make the building look like a gothic cathedral.

“It’s a masterpiece of radical, inside-out architecture,” says Mead, “representing London’s confidence and swagger.” From the street, she says, “it catches the attention and you wonder, ‘What could it be like inside?’” Mead has experienced the building first-hand: “My mum was an economics teacher and I joined one of her school trips to Lloyd’s 38 years ago. I remember then thinking it was huge.”

With all the infrastructure removed from the inside, the Lloyd’s building has capacity for a double-height space for the trading floor and a galleried atrium that reaches to the steel and glass barrel-vaulted roof, 14 floors above. Historian Reyner Banham compared the atrium to the Parthenon when he presented Rogers with the Royal Institute of British Architects’ gold medal in 1985.

The building also includes historical artefacts from Lloyd’s of London’s 338-year history. The Adam Room, originally designed in 1763 for Bowood House in Wiltshire by neoclassical architect Robert Adam, was sliced into 1,500 pieces in 1958 and moved to Lloyd’s HQ. The old library from Lloyds’ former home in the Cooper building on Leadenhall Street – designed by Sir Edwin Cooper in 1928 – was similarly salvaged. There is also a 1958 war memorial stained glass by artist Hugh Easton while, on the main trading floor, the Lutine Bell sits, hung within a mahogany, pillared temple. The bell, rescued from the wreck of HMS Lutine, has been used since 1858 to alert insurance underwriters to a maritime disaster. It’s still used to acknowledge ceremonial occasions such as Remembrance Sunday.

The Lloyd’s building’s place in British culture is nuanced. It appeared in 1986, the same year the City was deregulated, and came to symbolise that gear change to a voracious capitalist financial market shaped by international powers. The design’s references to industrialism and religion married to futurism invite ruminations about ideas of power in British history.

Architecturally, though, its reputation has endured. Not everyone is as damning as King Charles. Historian Geraint Franklin, of Historic England, who last year featured the building on the cover of his book High-Tech Britain, says it was designed to adapt and evolve. “Lloyd’s is flexible. Its services, lifts and even loos are mounted on the outside, freeing up the workplace inside. In recent years, the glazing has been renovated, carefully recutting the original ‘sparkle glass’.” This refers to textured glass panes that refract light so the building glitters in the sun.

“The main trading areas have been recently refurbished,” adds Franklin. “On paper, the plan is rational and diagrammatic, but it’s a dynamic, romantic exterior. Lloyd’s was never intended to be taken in at a single glance but to be encountered in snatched views from the streets. It’s obsessively detailed – with stainless steel, glass and white concrete making up a sharp City palette, highlighted by careful lighting.”

Mead is just pleased that more people will get to experience this. “In our programme of over 730 buildings, Lloyd’s is perhaps the greatest statement building. It’s heavyweight, look-at-me and counterintuitive. We’re all about the social impact that access brings – it gives people a sense of belonging to the city. Can’t wait to hear what they say about Lloyd’s.”

Tickets to Lloyd’s are free but must be booked in advance at openhouse. org. uk. Booking opens at noon tomorrow. London Open House festival runs 12-20 September.

The best packing cubes in the UK to save space and travel smarter – tested on real trips

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 14:00:48 GMT

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Whether you’re trying to squeeze more into a carry-on or simply want a tidier suitcase, our expert rounds up the top cubes, from compression to lightweight

The best suitcases for your next holiday

Nightmarish scenes reminiscent of a Hieronymus Bosch painting used to erupt whenever I travelled with a case. Skirts and shirt sleeves slithered out from under compression straps, worn clothes frolicked with unworn clothes in the lid compartment, and even the best suitcases would sometimes leave my clothing creased and jumbled.

Packing cubes have changed all that. Boxy, zippable and small to varying degrees, these organisation accessories are designed to keep items neat and separate inside a suitcase or bag.

Luggage organisation accessories have been around for decades, but only in recent years has interest in packing cubes boomed. Formerly the preserve of travel aficionados, they’re now part of mainstream travel, borne on a wave of social media recommendations and celebrity endorsements.

You’ll often find packing cubes sold as a set, with assorted sizes to suit different types of luggage (such as larger cubes for shirts, dresses or trousers, and smaller ones for socks and underwear). Most are a soft-sided cuboid shape, so packing cube is a misnomer. Some brands call them “packing cells”.

As products go, packing cubes are not especially varied, but you may still notice meaningful differences between them. Some are slightly more rigid; some are made from smarter-looking or softer materials; and some have special features, such as double-zippered compression packing cubes, which squeeze air out to save space.

I tested 14 of the best packing cube sets (and related products such as shoe bags) to help you solve your own particular packing puzzles. The best 11 are reviewed below.

Best packing cubes overallJuly Packing cells, four pack

Best budget packing cubesM&S Packing cubes, five pack

Best packing cubes with sectionsStubble & Co Packing cubes, three pack

Best compression packing cubesAntler Stripe packing cubes, four pack

Best shoe storageTroubadour Elemental shoe bag

There are few travel essentials I’ve yet to review for the Filter. My travel pillow testing took me aboard trains, buses and arcade machines; I reviewed cabin bags by hauling them over an assault course; and I’ve applied a similar spirit of adventurous rigour to assessing the packing cubes featured here.

I’ve been testing products for this publication and others for the past decade, as well as writing articles on travel and other topics. On the rare and serene occasions when product samples aren’t whizzing in and out of my home, I like to explore this country and – when I’m lucky enough – others. The reviews below are all grounded in real travel experiences.

I tested the packing cubes during a period in which I had staycations and work trips around England planned, so that I’d have the opportunity to field-test everything while travelling. I packed the cubes with appropriately sized items and assessed their ability to keep clothing neat and crease-free.

For a sterner test, I made sure to jostle each set of packing cubes inside my suitcase or bag, then noted how well the items inside had retained their stored shape. There’s no doubt that subjective factors such as feel and aesthetic also play into the appeal of a packing cube, so I’ve referenced these considerations where noteworthy.

Most of the brands didn’t need their packing cubes back after testing. These review units have been donated for fundraising to Cat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.

Between the four cubes in this set – two large, one medium and one small – there’s ample scope to store different types of clothing separately. The large cubes are best for shirts, while smaller items can roll or fold up neatly into the medium and small ones.

Why we love themI put some smart shirts and trousers into these packing cubes, slung them into a duffel bag and travelled well over 200 miles by bus, train and ferry, stopping to add a secondhand cat ornament to my luggage along the way. At the end of all this, I was impressed to find that the cubes had kept the clothes crease-free and neatly folded, just as they were when I packed them.

The cubes themselves are simple and nicely finished. On the sides and base, the material is shiny and smooth, with a fine texture providing some grip for stored items. A mesh top layer provides breathability and easy identification of which clothes are in which cube, while the double zipper feels decent quality.

It’s a shame that … you may find that these are a little too soft to keep some items straight and orderly, especially when you don’t have enough suitable clothing to fill a cube – or if your luggage will have to go through the ordeal of an aeroplane’s hold.

Why we love themIf you haven’t used compression packing cubes before, you’re in for a treat. The second zipper does a great job of squishing the cubes, making a meaningful difference to their size and the luggage space they take up.

Among Antler’s many packing cube designs, I particularly liked this stripy green colourway, which features the brand’s Icon Stripe motif on the expandable sides and base of each cube. The Thule Chasm small gear cube offers added protection to valuables or items vulnerable to water damage, with a weather-resistant tarp fabric and polyurethane-coated zippers to limit water ingress.

I used this cube to keep my travel documents and smartphone safe while travelling in poor weather. Type: standard packing cube set; other options: no; sizes included (WDH): small (11 x 10 x 26cm); medium (20.5 x 10 x 26cm); large (32 x 10 x 17.5cm); extra-large (26 x 10 x 32cm); colours available: two; materials: recycled PET plastic

Best for: young children

It never hurts to have more otter-themed items in your life. This packing cube set from LittleLife is particularly endearing, with a lovely print and materials and dimensions designed to suit very young children.

I’m contentedly babyless, but two of my friends are parents to a cherubic infant and took this set for a spin. They found it useful for carrying baby care items day to day, as well as for bigger adventures. Importantly, the materials are wipe-clean.

It didn’t make the final cut because … some parents may prefer to buy a generic packing cube set for their child to use for longer.

Type: children’s packing cube set; other options: no; sizes included (WH): 2 x small pouches (23 x 17cm); large pouch (25 x 22cm); small case (20 x 15cm); large case (30 x 20cm); colours available: one; materials: polyester

Testing for this article taught me that the most important consideration is to make sure your packing cube is filled close to capacity. This prevents items from moving around and getting creased inside the cube, which would limit its usefulness. If you’re using a compression packing cube, this is somewhat less relevant, as you can shrink the cube down to suit its contents.

Packing cubes are ideal for travellers who like to fold smart clothes flat, as they can help them stay folded. Of course, you can roll clothes up inside them if you prefer. There’s more than one way to pack a cube.

If you want to pack as much as possible into your suitcase, then a set of compression cubes could save you a little space (relative to ordinary ones).

Typically, compression packing cubes have two zippers – one to seal your items inside, and another that allows you to squeeze the cube into a tighter form. Close the first zipper, squish the packing cube down until you’re satisfied, then do up the second zipper.

A more extreme option, generally reserved for lengthy trips or moving home, is a vacuum bag, which uses a vacuum cleaner to remove air and compress your belongings. Unlike a compression packing cube, however, you can’t open and reseal whenever you need something during your journey.

Packing cubes are perhaps at their most useful inside a backpack, where solutions for organising clothes are often limited. I use a packing cube inside my day-to-day backpack to keep my five-a-side football kit separate from non-sweaty things. I’ve also started taking a few of them on multiday hikes and camping trips – one or two for fresh clothes, and one or two for grubby ones.

Some packing accessories are pouch-shaped, which are arguably more convenient for a backpack than blocky packing cubes, especially if you want something to store flip-flops or casual shoes for your downtime.

Particularly large packing cubes may not be suitable for backpacks, as it may be difficult to fit them inside the bag or through its opening.

One person dead and more than 200 ill in UK salmonella outbreak

The Guardian Tue, 18 Aug 2026 13:08:58 GMT

UKHSA rules out British produce as source of infections and says evidence points to consumption of imported eggs

One person has died and more than 200 others have fallen ill during a UK-wide outbreak of salmonella that health officials have linked to people eating imported eggs.

The 207 people affected range in age from under one year to 90 years old, according to the UK Health Security Agency, which is leading an investigation into the outbreak.

They appear to have consumed the contaminated eggs in cafes and restaurants, rather than at home.

The UKHSA has ruled out UK-produced eggs or poultry as the source and said the available evidence pointed to eggs imported into Britain. It is working with other European countries, through their joint system of surveillance of threats to health, to identify how the outbreak began.

The agency said it could not release any details of the person who died or circumstances of their death because it was the subject of a continuing investigation.

It said at least 34 people were left so ill with salmonellosis, the illness caused by salmonella, that they had to be treated in hospital, and two had a bloodstream infection.

Officials have ascertained through whole-genome sequencing that all 207 cases are linked to a single strain of salmonella. The first case was identified on 11 August 2025, but most of them have been identified since the middle of last month.

Most of the cases have been in England (199), six in Scotland and one each in Wales and Northern Ireland. London has had 47 cases so far and the Yorkshire and the Humber region 38 cases.

“This isn’t an isolated incident. This outbreak is closely related to one from 2025 that was also linked to imported eggs, with the identified strain genetically similar between the two years,” said Dr Safi Rehman, a research associate at King’s College London.

UKHSA’s notice alerting the public to the outbreak, issued on Tuesday morning, said: “Extensive epidemiological and food chain investigations are ongoing to identify the source and origin of the contamination responsible for illness.”

Interviews with 114 of those left ill have identified “five food businesses where two or more independent cases reported attending in the week prior to symptom onset. These food businesses link 24 cases in total.” The agency did not name the five businesses.

It added: “Food chain investigations to date have identified that these premises are supplied by eggs from multiple sources, including egg importers. Local investigations have also identified possible cross-contamination risk events within two of these settings. At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry.”

Hannah Charles, the agency’s lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections, said: “We’re working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.

“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person to person. Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.

“Symptoms of a salmonella infection include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out-of-hours service in the first instance.”

She advised the public to take action to prevent the spread of salmonella. “Wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and, if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible.”
