Zyzz Was the Original Looksmaxxer. His Rise and Untimely Death Feel More Relevant Than Ever

Wired August 15, 2026

“We’re all gonna make it, brah!”

That was the aspirational rallying cry of Aziz Shavershian, better known by his online alias, Zyzz. Once the shy and skinny son of Kurdish parents who struggled to find his place in Sydney, Australia, where the family had moved from Russia, he’d thrown himself wholeheartedly into fitness, spending hours at the gym every day and frequenting the infamous Bodybuilding. com and 4chan forums.

In time, the teenager’s chiseled physique gave him the confidence to develop an online persona that had little in common with the gentle and goofy kid that his friends and family knew. This would be Zyzz, a brash raver who strutted, mugged, danced, and flexed shirtless in front of his webcam while asking if viewers were “mirin’” (that is, admiring his body) and exhorting other men to chase their self-improvement goals. By 2010, his videos had made him an Australian celebrity with fans around the globe.

And as of August 2011, he was dead in Thailand, at the age of 22.

Aziz “Zyzz” Shavershian and brother Said “Chestbrah” Shavershian.

Shavershian’s brief and tragic life is the basis of a new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, now available on Apple TV and Prime Video. But this keenly nuanced film is more than the familiar tale of an ambitious youth who pursued fame at all costs. It also reckons with the digital forces that could produce a person like Zyzz in the first place, and how his preternatural instincts for navigating a brand-new media ecosystem anticipated an entire generation of masculinity influencers.

Depending on your perspective, Zyzz can be regarded as the original “looksmaxxer”—though the term had yet to be coined—or one of the earliest forefathers of the manosphere as we know it today.

“I really see this as a cautionary tale,” Poster Boy’s director, Selina Miles, tells WIRED. She notes that Shavershian’s meteoric rise and untimely death left a huge impression on Australian millennials, and that his legend continues to reverberate today. “He had his transformation, and his story has really resonated with a lot of people,” she says. “We have to stay curious as to why. Why has he had this impact on men?”

Through a mixture of Zyzz’s archival content and interviews with close friends as well as his older brother, Said Shavershian—a professional bodybuilder to this day—the documentary circles the question of his outsized appeal during a key shift in human communications. At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success. Indeed, Zyzz’s earliest videos amount to little more than a kid playing around in his bedroom; later, he and his pals experimented with showing off their abs and biceps at music festivals and nightlife hot spots, hoping for reactions of any kind.

While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion and mutual support for men looking to become the best version of themselves, he also began to feed off those who insulted him, online and off: “U mad?” and “Come at me brah” were two of his recurring catchphrases. He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters. “He made this page on Facebook that was, like, ‘10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz,’” Miles says, describing an incident that didn’t make it into the documentary’s final cut. “When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.”

His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist, contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form. A 2010 post on his Facebook page read: “id rather be dead than ‘normal.’”

By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.

Behind the bravado, however, Zyzz seemed psychologically unprepared for the limelight. In addition to using steroids to sculpt his Renaissance-worthy physique (he and the fitness personalities in his orbit were known as the “Aesthetics Crew”), he took Xanax to deal with the stress and paranoia that came with being mobbed in public, where he was also frequently menaced by young men looking for a fight.

And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines, his own methods grew ever more extreme. In one video, he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance despite the likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.

Today, manosphere streamers and podcasters can make millions hawking supplements and classes to vulnerable young men looking to take charge of their life in one way or another. Zyzz, Miles says, was “right on the cusp” of that economy, reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators. “It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme,” she says.

Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer to decide the extent to which Zyzz served as a template for the likes of misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, who flashes onscreen in one sequence. (He and his brother, Tristan Tate, are currently fighting extradition from the US to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking that their attorney has claimed are without merit.) Setting aside some provocative aspects of behavior, Zyzz did not appear to preach from a place of nihilism or cynicism, and he had a genuine community.

“Aziz did have friends, and I think that male friendship is one of the beautiful themes of this story,” Miles says, referring to the members of the Aesthetics Crew who sat for interviews and remain in touch today. She wonders if they collectively make the case that a currently voguish explanation for radicalization among men, the so-called male loneliness epidemic, “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.” In the end, she notes, it was Zyzz who isolated himself from this network as they sought to help him.

Zyzz traveled alone to Thailand in July 2011, having told each of his closest friends that he was traveling with another one of them. After his death, Thai authorities revealed that he purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and underwent multiple facial surgeries while in the country. Those who went to identify his body upon its return to Australia recount how they could barely recognize him due to those procedures.

The exact cause of Shavershian’s death was never made public until Poster Boy disclosed the findings of his toxicology report: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines.

Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized as a martyr for the manosphere. The closing credits of the film show a montage of tattoos in his memory. His brother Said, who runs a fitness brand, sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.” (He continues to follow Zyzz’s playbook when it comes to courting controversy, too, and is shown recording a podcast in which he argues that there is “no such thing as toxic masculinity.”)

But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons from what happened to Shavershian as he evolved into Zyzz, fracturing his real identity in the process of building up the kind of facade that is all too common in the influencer age he prefigured.

“This was this persona that he created, and he felt that it was separate from who he really was, that it was OK to take risks,” Miles says. “It was so successful, and it did kind of take over his life.” Whatever good intentions and ideals he may have had, the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,” she says.

Yet his formula has clearly endured. There are still a lot of young men who want to hear “that you can be the master of your own universe, you can have some control over your fate, and you can be who you wanna be,” Miles says. “More than ever, men are seeking that sense of hope. And Zyzz kind of gave that to them.”

I Tested the Best Apple Watch Bands for Every Occasion

Wired August 15, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Apple Watches are smart little gadgets, but they don't always fit the vibe. There were plenty of nights when I left mine at home because, as much as I wanted to check my notifications discreetly, the watch just didn't match my outfit. I've also had my fair share of faux pas and just let the neon orange sport band clash with my neutral ensemble.

Fortunately, Apple Watch bands are a simple and relatively affordable way to zhuzh up the look of your wearable. Beyond aesthetics, different styles also impact performance and functionality. For example, I don't want a heavy stainless steel or high-quality leather band weighing me down during a sweaty workout, just as I wouldn't wear a flimsy silicone band to a dinner party.

At WIRED, we've been testing bands since the very first Apple Watch launched in 2015. After years of wearing and swapping, I've rounded up the best bands for every occasion. Be sure to check out our related product guides, including the Best Apple Watch Accessories, Best Apple Watch, and Best Smartwatches for more recommendations.

Apple

Nomad

Amazon

Konsu NYC

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Updated August 2026: I added a comparison chart, along with the Apple Sport Band to Honorable Mentions. Prices and links were also updated.

How I Test Apple Watch Bands

I research Apple Watch bands across major retailers, including Apple, Amazon, and Nike. I also consulted former WIRED editor Adrienne So, who had covered fitness trackers and Apple Watch bands for a decade. I look for bestsellers, affordable dupes, and niche finds.

I test Apple Watch bands all day, every day, across workouts, commutes, and overnight. Each band is worn for at least two weeks and subjected to sweat, water, and everyday friction. That's typically enough time to evaluate comfort, quality, and durability. If it's severely uncomfortable or triggers skin irritation on the first day of testing, it is ruled out. My top picks remain in my rotation for months so I can compare them against newer models and assess how they hold up over time.

Most of the Apple Watch bands remain in storage so I can continue long-term testing and compare newer releases against older models. Any discontinued models are donated once testing is complete.

What Am I Testing Next?

I'm testing the Nomad Sport Band. I'm also reevaluating the Nomad Tempo Band, the Apple Trail Loop, and the Apple Milanese Titanium Band.

Nike

Apple

The Nike Sport Loop has been my everyday band since 2020. I bought another in 2023 because I wanted to swap colors, and I figured after three years, I should buy a brand-new one, but it has held up remarkably well. Made from a blend of recycled polyester, spandex, and nylon, it's breathable and lightweight. The double-layered nylon weave is designed with dense loops that help prevent moisture from getting trapped against your skin. As long as you regularly hand-wash it to rid it of sweat buildup and dirt, it stays odor-free.

The hook-and-loop fastener and pull tab make it easy to adjust with one hand. It is Velcro, so beware—it can snag on softer fabrics. Still, for a band designed with sports in mind, it's understated enough to wear almost anywhere. I wouldn't wear it to a formal event, but for the office or casual social events, it's perfect.

Nomad

Nomad

Nomad originally designed the Stratos Band for the Apple Watch Ultra, but it fits just as well with the SE and Series 1 through 11. It's easy to adjust, refined enough for the office, and backed by Grade 4 titanium hardware with a scratch-resistant DLC coating. FKM rubber links (PFA-free and antimicrobial, according to Nomad) add flexibility, durability, and water resistance. The clasp is made with corrosion-resistant N52 magnets, which make it effortless to snap on, and it's designed with a manual release button, so you don't have to worry about it accidentally falling off. It's technically suited for workouts and outdoor use, but it is a hefty band that I personally prefer for casual everyday wear.

The hardware comes in natural or black finishes, which is nice if you're particular about matching your setup. The FKM rubber comes in four different colorways, including a limited-edition icy blue that glows in the dark. The glow effect is short-lived (roughly 10 to 20 minutes), and based on online feedback, more of a novelty than a standout feature.

Moft

Amazon

Moft's Snap Duo Watch Band is made from nontoxic, food-grade silicone, but you wouldn't know it at a glance. The pebbled finish mimics leather, giving it a more elevated look, without the stiffness or upkeep. Also, unlike leather, it's noticeably soft, waterproof, and resistant to direct, which makes it just as suitable for workouts and water sports as it is for the office.

The design is particularly interesting. Each band features two colors, and thanks to a bidirectional connector, you can flip and swap sides to create four different looks. Switching it up is easy, and the magnetic link is even easier to snap on. Keep in mind, there's no manual release mechanism, so it may not feel sturdy on its own. Moft includes a removable buckle as an extra precaution, and while it takes a bit of fiddling to attach, it's worth using for a more secure fit.

Konsu NYC

Konsu NYC

Former WIRED editor Adrienne So says the Moher Green—inspired by Ireland's Cliffs of Moher—is the most beautiful band she's ever worn. The color is rich, but Konsu NYC also offers seven other colors that are just as vibrant. The top and bottom layers are 100 percent top-grain calfskin leather, and the middle layer is a proprietary, thin fiber that the company claims is 15 times stronger than steel. The hardware is 316-grade stainless steel that is laser etched, machine polished, and PVD coated, which makes it scratch- and corrosion-resistant. You can also customize the adapter and buckle finishes to be either silver, gold, or black.

Apple

Apple

Hermes

I purchased the Hermés band last year after the orange Alpine Loop on my Ultra got too sooty to continue into a third year of honorable service. The Hermés band is an equally loud orange, but no one ever asks about it; it's relatively discreet as luxury goods go. Installation is a breeze, and the color comes close to matching the titanium case, with a tad extra silvery shine.

The fluoroelastomer feels soft but sturdy against the skin and washes better than the Alpine Loop. I especially like the brand-stamped quick-release clasp (deployment buckle), which makes it a breeze to take on or off with a quick squeeze on the sides. It runs large, and I would not recommend it to people with small wrists, as I'm a large man and using the third of seven notches. After a year of daily wear, there is a little darkening around the clasp from my dragging my wrists around my desk, but that's the part of the band that the fewest people see. —Martin Cizmar

Apple Sport Band for $49: The Sport Band is decent—I’m wearing it right now—and its sweat-resistant fluoroelastomer makes it a solid choice for workouts and anyone who wants a low-maintenance band they can easily wipe clean. The pin-and-tuck closure doesn’t offer as much adjustability as I’d like. My usual setting feels a little too loose for workouts when I want accurate tracking, but tightening it one notch is uncomfortable. Also, if you’re trying to avoid fluoroelastomer, I’d skip this one for now. Apple has said it’s working to phase out PFAs from its products, but that transition will take time.

Apple Milanese Titanium Band for $199: The Apple Watch Ultra 2 came in a black finish, which was matched by this special black titanium Milanese loop. The standout feature is the parachute-style buckle, which Apple claims was historically used for diving and other underwater activities. (I seem to remember that most water activities use ratchet tie downs and threaded cam buckles for straps, but I will let this slide.) The titanium doesn't irritate my skin, and the band and buckle smooth and easy to adjust. It's carbon-neutral, and it turns your sporty watch into a much dressier watch. —Adrienne So

Apple Trail Loop for $99: Apple has several band varieties for different activities: the Alpine Loop ($99) for outdoor adventures, the Ocean Band ($99) for water sports, and the Trail Loop for endurance runs and hikes.

Nomad Tempo Band for $59: If you must have a fluoroelastomer band, the Tempo bands are PFAS-free. It's slightly too big for my 150-mm wrist, and Nomad hedges its bets with sizing by making each band backward-compatible with two sizes; for example, the smallest size is compatible with both 41- and 42-mm watch sizes. This doesn't quite work if you have the older, smaller-size watch, but it fits my 46-mm Series 10 well. —Adrienne So

Wrangler Ranch Rider Calf Hair Band for $35: This collaboration between Wrangler and accessory company WithIt includes seven bands of all different materials, from a turquoise-and-silver bracelet band to a denim band. I was unexpectedly charmed by the Rodeo Ready, which is made from calf hair that has been bleached and dyed. It can be sized to fit all Apple Watch models, from the older 38-mm versions to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. It is comfortable and tacky—in a good way—especially if you're wearing a bunch of silver bangles and beads and patting a horse. —Adrienne So

Zzdzz Silicone Magnetic Strap for $20: My Instagram feed is bombarded with ads for easy-to-put-on adjustable silicone straps, so I bought this cheap one off Amazon. The colors are vibrant, and it is, indeed, very comfortable and easy to adjust. However, the flip side of that is that it falls off very easily, and I can't vouch for its durability. Also, the little loop that holds the strap down isn't attached to the band at any point, so I lose it constantly. Whatever—it's less than $20. —Adrienne So

Apple Solo Loop for $49: Apple really hawks its precisely sized Solo Loops, which form a single loop around your wrist. But they're expensive, and as an active person, I can't size them correctly. They're always too tight when I'm working out and too loose when I'm not. I prefer an adjustable band. —Adrienne So

Hopo Resin Band for $13: My mom has this gorgeous Machete Apple Watch tortoiseshell resin bracelet band ($80), so I figured I'd do her one better and order the cheap one off Amazon. It's a no-go—the included pin remover is too short, so I can't take links out to make the band smaller. I will just get the Machete band next time. —Adrienne So

Puerto Rico Is Rationing Water. It Could’ve Avoided It by Harvesting Rainwater

Wired August 15, 2026

Puerto Rico is experiencing a historic drought that’s led to water rationing following the driest month on record in July.

Yet one ready-made solution is barely being tapped: the normally copious rainfall. Anywhere from 30 to 169 inches of precipitation falls on the territory annually, but the government doesn't require US citizens in Puerto Rico to install catchment systems to take advantage of the free resource—unlike some other island states. As climate change increases the odds of more intense droughts on the island, that type of decentralized infrastructure may be just what Puerto Ricans need in an emergency.

“One of the best unused reservoirs of water in Puerto Rico are the roofs of the houses,” says Fernando Abruña, a partner at local firm Abruña & Musgrave Architects.

The drought has exacerbated a water crisis that was already in motion due to ruptured water pipes and other decrepit infrastructure. For the past week, Puerto Rico governor Jenniffer González has ordered municipal governments to shut off water two days at a time for people in the northeast to conserve local supplies, leaving 180,000 households with limited access. The problems began well before that, though: Many families have been without consistent water for more than 100 days.

While the drought is a factor, the biggest issue isn’t a lack of water, says environmental lawyer Ruth Santiago, but rather the government’s mismanagement of it.

“Even with the climate crisis and these droughts, we still have abundant water,” says Santiago, who works with the local group Comité Diálogo Ambiental (the Environmental Dialogue Committee). “We could be harvesting rainwater right now,” she says as a storm erupts mid-conversation.

The most resilient harvesting systems rely on gravity, using gutters to divert rainwater from a roof to a canister that connects to indoor pipes like a faucet or showerhead. Bigger systems can help collect water to cool power plants and other industrial uses.

Abruña, who is also a fellow with the American Institute of Architects, estimates the island could gather 30 billion gallons of water a year if just 1 million households used rainwater collection technology. The average resident uses 62 gallons a day, amounting to just over 72 billion gallons of residential water use a year.

The Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority loses about 60 percent of the island’s drinking water before any arrives at customers’ homes due to leaking pipes and failing infrastructure. The ongoing emergency was caused, in part, by a series of ruptures in the 72-inch Superaqueduct water pipe, a main artery that services major cities on the northern coast. Repairing and updating the island’s aging water distribution system is most urgent, Santiago says, but rainwater harvesting is a cost-effective solution that can be quickly implemented.

The practice is not widespread in Puerto Rico, where the government has prioritized centralized grids fed by freshwater, but these systems are popular in other island communities. Roughly 90 percent of homes in the US Virgin Islands have a cistern to collect rainwater, and the territory has building codes that require many new developments to include this infrastructure. (Barbados has similar codes.) In Hawaii, Honolulu County even offers a limited number of free rain barrel installations to residents.

“There is nothing that can help the Caribbean region as quickly and as reliably as rainwater harvesting,” says Farah Nibbs, an assistant professor at the University of Maryland Baltimore County’s Department of Emergency and Disaster Health Systems, noting governments should treat it “as part of the national water supply.”

She also says governments should help cover the costs to avoid putting onerous “economic and financial burdens on households.” Yet in Puerto Rico, the government offers no incentives or financial assistance. That’s left small organizations attempting to meet demand.

Since 2010, local environmental nonprofit Plenitud Puerto Rico has donated and installed 73 rainwater harvesting systems for neighbors in Las Marías, a mountainous municipality on the western side of Puerto Rico. Executive codirector Owen Ingley estimates that the technology costs the group $500 to $2,000 for small, simple units and up to $5,000 for larger, more advanced ones with electric pumps. There are also additional costs to maintain the system, especially if a bad storm damages it, and to monitor water quality.

The team recently installed a unit for a man in his eighties who lives alone and regularly experiences disruptions to his water supply. The system doesn’t provide drinking water, but it helps him meet other household needs such as flushing the toilet or filling his dog’s water bowl. “He’s a really sweet and talkative guy with gray hair and a big smile,” Ingley says.

José Pérez Cordero, an at-large legislator in the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, introduced a resolution in June that would order the Puerto Rican Natural Resources Committee to conduct a feasibility study on rainwater harvesting. That would include looking at how other Caribbean islands have made it work and adopting similar models for Puerto Rico. The proposal has gone nowhere, even as water insecurity mounts.

“We are, right now, in the perfect moment to do it, because we are in the middle of a crisis,” Pérez Cordero says. “Sadly, we always wait for the reaction.”

He points to a 2024 law that mandated all public agencies to implement rainwater collection systems on government buildings. That, too, has gone nowhere: Agencies aren’t following the law, nor is it being enforced. Pérez Cordero’s New Progressive Party is in power, but he says his peers have often lacked the political will to be proactive and prioritize the environment.

Rainwater harvesting won’t solve all of Puerto Rico’s water problems, particularly in urban locations where it’s hard to install them in large apartment complexes. They also aren’t sustainable if the wet season isn’t rainy enough—a prospect that’s likely to increase as burning fossil fuels heats up the planet. But that doesn’t mean they can’t play a role in shoring up a dysfunctional system.

“Facing climate change, every year is going to be harder,” Pérez Cordero says. “Every year, the dry season is going to be longer. Every year, the rainy season is going to be harder too.”

Amazon Can Use Your Twitch Content to Train Its AI—Unless You Opt Out

Wired August 15, 2026

Twitch has updated its account settings to let streamers opt out of having their content used to help train the artificial intelligence models of Twitch’s parent company, Amazon.

Although the move has reassured some creators, it remains unclear exactly when the streaming platform began using the posts, streams, and videos of its users to train Amazon’s systems. The revelation is raising new concerns about how big tech companies handle their users’ data.

The opt-out process is simple. From the Twitch website or mobile app, click on your account avatar, select Settings, and then go to the Security and Privacy section in the menu. There, you’ll find the Generative AI Training option, where you can disable the use of your content for that purpose.

In the language next to the toggle, Twitch notes that “disabling this option does not prevent Twitch and Amazon from using your channel’s content for other purposes described in Twitch’s Privacy Notice.” These include AI-powered platform features designed to facilitate streamers’ growth and monetization, such as real-time assistance for sponsorship campaigns, viewer discovery through recommendations, and community safety via tools like AutoMod.

The new setting aims to recognize creators’ right to decide how the content they produce is used. However, its launch has also raised questions about how Twitch and Amazon have used that content up to now.

In a forum dedicated to the topic, more than 16,000 creators expressed opposition to having their content being used by default to train Amazon’s AI systems—a practice that only came to light following the update to the settings.

The backlash arose after a livestream in which Mary Kish, Twitch’s head of community, explained the introduction of the changes. The executive acknowledged that the change would provoke a negative reaction. Mike Minton, Twitch’s head of product, also noted—in what he described as “a candid response”—that keeping the option to use content for AI training enabled by default was necessary, since otherwise “no one would participate” in the process.

Minton pointed out that these mechanisms are not unique to Twitch and considered it likely that other companies developing AI systems are also extracting content from Twitch and other services to use in training their models. “I don’t know for sure,” he said, “but I think it’s quite reasonable to assume that almost any publicly available content is used to train models in one way or another, with or without permission. So I think we also need to acknowledge that there’s a lot here that’s beyond even our direct control.”

These statements raised new questions: Since when has Twitch content been used to train AI models? Is Amazon the only company using this data, or are its business partners also involved? To what extent and in what ways is the authorship of content published by creators respected?

Twitch’s Terms of Service, in effect since March 2024, have stipulated that users grant Twitch and its sublicensees the right to use, reproduce, modify, adapt, distribute, and create derivative works from their content. However, until now, they have not explicitly stated that such materials could be used to train generative AI models.

This case highlights one of the major challenges facing AI system developers: the growing shortage of high-quality data for training models.

Although companies like OpenAI have reached agreements with various publishers (including WIRED’s corporate parent, Condé Nast) to use some of their content for this purpose, available data sources are dwindling as technology advances and the demand for data increases. As a result, various alternatives have emerged that are reigniting the debate over the ethics and transparency of training processes.

For some time now, Meta has been using posts and images that users share on Facebook and Instagram to train its AI models. Recently, it also came to light that the company was using its employees’ activity and screenshots captured by users of its smart glasses for the same purpose. Similar cases have been documented involving Google and YouTube.

Thus, high-quality training data has become another strategic resource—along with chips, memory, and electricity—that the leading developers of artificial intelligence models have found running short as they struggle to sustain the pace of innovation demanded by the market. All signs point to a portion of that demand being met with information generated by users themselves, in exchange for free access to everyday digital services.

This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Google Workspace Promo Codes for August 2026

Wired August 15, 2026

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of if you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access – basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i. e. update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and it can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized to Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow up message. No apps or links are needed.

What Is El Niño, and What Does It Mean for Weather, Water, and the Global Economy?

Wired August 17, 2026

El Niño looks to reach an intensity unprecedented in recorded history.

Characterized by warmer-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific, El Niño occurs every few years. Meteorological agencies and researchers around the world are on high alert because when the heat stored in the ocean is released into the atmosphere, it triggers a chain reaction that affects rainfall, temperatures, and even hurricane activity around the world.

This year’s El Niño has gained strength at an exceptional speed, and it will wreak havoc on everything from fisheries to ski seasons. Not all impacts are bad—the parched Southwest, for example, is likely to see more winter precipitation—but anticipating them is the key to being prepared.

What exactly is happening now, and what might happen in the coming months? Read on to understand what El Niño is, why this one might be a super El Niño, and where its impacts will be most acutely felt.

Declaring an El Niño requires meeting a certain threshold of oceanic heat in the Pacific—specifically, a region known as Niño 3.4. It’s an area that sits between Niño 3 and Niño 4 if you want to geek out even more. In plain language, it’s a region in the eastern-central tropical Pacific.

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration uses the three-month average sea surface temperature of the region to determine if an El Niño is in effect. If the ocean is 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal for three overlapping three-month periods, it’s officially an El Niño.

Other weather agencies do things a little differently. Japan’s Meteorological Agency monitors a slightly different region using its own criteria, while the Australian Bureau of Meteorology’s threshold has an atmospheric component as well.

In addition to warmer oceans, the trade winds that blow from east to west also weaken. That allows seawater to pile up on the eastern side of the Pacific. In 1997 and 2015—when El Niño events were among the strongest on record—sea levels rose more than 18 centimeters (7 inches) above average.

All this increases the odds of shifts in weather around the world. There’s the aforementioned increase in rainfall in the Southwest as well as a corresponding decrease in Pacific Northwest precipitation. Atlantic hurricane season tends to be milder as well, with fewer storms.

Indonesia sees an increased risk of drought, as do parts of southern Africa. El Niño also tends to raise the odds of winter warmth in Japan and parts of Australia and Brazil. (We can only speak of probabilities, because El Niño is not the only phenomenon affecting the weather on a given day or in a given season, but the phenomenon tilts the odds.

“Super El Niño” isn’t an official term any meteorological agency uses, but scientists generally use it to define any event where temperatures rise by at least 2 degrees Celsius above average. While there’s no standardized definition, four particular El Niños are ones that check the super box: 1982–83, 1997–98, 2015–16, and 2023–24.

When the Super El Niño occurred in 1982–83, the Colorado River Basin in the US was hit by record-breaking heavy snowfall. Combined with high spring temperatures and rainfall, the river’s flow exceeded 1.5 times the average. Reservoirs upstream filled to capacity one after another, forcing emergency releases, and Lake Mead also reached near-capacity, causing water to overflow from the Hoover Dam spillway for the first time in about 40 years. As a result, the basin suffered significant flood damage. In other words, the impacts of El Niño that may be “good” can still lead to bad outcomes.

In 1997–98, Indonesia was hit by the worst drought in the past half-century, while the 2023-24 super El Niño contributed to the worst drought in over 100 years for southern Africa. Conditions were so extreme that approximately 61 million people needed humanitarian aid.

There is a greater than 90 percent probability of this El Niño becoming “very strong” this fall and winter, according to NOAA.

Modeling by Berkeley Earth shows that median temperatures for the Niño 3.4 region could reach 3.6 degrees Celsius above normal—even after accounting for the effects of long-term global warming. This would exceed the all-time high recorded during the 2015–16 El Niño by approximately 0.8 degrees Celsius. Given that the difference between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Niño events over the past 150 years was only about 0.5 degrees Celsius, this represents an exceptional level of warming.

This El Niño event is also developing at a faster pace than usual. While the 2015 El Niño developed from a situation where sea surface temperatures were already rising, this year’s began in a state closer to a La Niña (more on that later), with below-average sea surface temperatures. Nevertheless, it is said to be developing even more rapidly than the 1997–98 super El Niño.

The economic impact of El Niño cannot be overlooked either. An analysis found that the 1997–98 El Niño resulted in a cumulative loss of approximately $5.7 trillion over the following five years.

The counterpart to El Niño is La Niña, which is characterized by cooler-than-normal ocean temperatures in the Pacific. It also occurs every few years, and the effects are generally opposite to those of El Niño. That includes higher odds of more rain in Indonesia, a more active Atlantic hurricane season, and drier conditions in the Southwest, among others. But with El Niño likely in the driver’s seat until at least spring, those impacts aren’t the ones to watch out for.

This R-Rated Film Studio Wants to Be the HBO of AI

Wired August 17, 2026

Demand for artificially generated smut is surging. But the quality of the visual content being created and shared—like on companion apps, where adult performers are selling their likeness to give fans a 24/7 experience, WIRED reported in March—isn’t exactly movie-level caliber.

Rogue Studio, a cinematic AI-generator platform built around adult visual storytelling, is trying to change that. Launching today, the studio, which bills itself as a “playground for creative ethical mischief,” plans to deliver industry-level video production without creative and sexual restrictions. Its marquee product is Rogue 1.0, an AI video-generation tool for making uncensored adult content that is comparable to other pro-level models Hollywood is using.

“There really isn’t a place for a sophisticated creator to go make content that’s rated R. Either they go to these skeezy NSFW sites that are built on outdated open-source tech, or they try to do high-quality stuff but they’re censored up the gills,” a Rogue Studio cofounder, who goes by Mr. Rogue, tells WIRED. “It’s a very fine line between being a sophisticated platform for adults versus becoming just a porn site. And we do not want the latter. We want to do what HBO did for television.”

Rogue, which has subscription tiers ranging from $29 to $299, offers all the safe-for-work frontier models within its system—similar to Higgsfield, it includes NanoBanana, Seedance, Kling 2.0, and others—in addition to its own proprietary models for generating adult-oriented images and video. Using the platform, you can employ multiple elements from several different AI-generator models when drumming up ideas.

Let’s say you have a concept for a freaky sci-fi horror short. You could potentially start ideating on a zombie character using Midjourney, then use Rogue’s AI tools to add more high-definition uncensored features to the character.

According to its terms of service, Rogue prohibits user-generated images or videos for training, and it strictly forbids the creation or distribution of nonconsensual deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, unauthorized depictions of public figures, and other illegal or abusive imagery.

In an effort to prevent bad actors from using the platform to make these prohibited visuals, Rogue has three layers of human moderation. The first is at the prompt level, which searches for keywords and flags them for possible account suspension if it is determined that there is clear illegal intent. The next layer is inside the system, called the intention layer. Bad actors might try to outsmart moderators by slightly misspelling a real actor’s name to generate a deepfake image, so moderators will reread the prompt to assess the user’s intent. The final layer analyzes the image or video created before it is shared with the user. For example, if a user prompts “famous blonde singer” and the image generated looks like Taylor Swift, the image won’t get delivered.

Mr. Rogue tells WIRED that he and his fellow cofounder, both of whom are movie producers, have decided not to disclose their names because of the “real risk” involved in being associated with creating erotic-themed work. “Because of the climate right now in Hollywood and working in AI, you have got to be very careful,” Mr. Rogue says. (WIRED verified that the pair of founders do, in fact, work in Hollywood; they have produced movies with a combined box office of over $2 billion.)

In the wake of the 2023 Hollywood strikes, where labor unions fought to secure guardrails against the unapproved digital likenesses of actors appearing in films and TV, leading studios have been assessing ways to incorporate AI into productions with the goal of lowering expenses.

The friction has led to AI being seen as unfavorable and has created a stigma around it. Rogue’s cofounders know this but don’t want to shy away from the tech’s creative potential.

The reality is that AI is no longer a distant possibility for Hollywood. Computers are already working behind the scenes to animate preproduction storyboards and create a more efficient editing process, such as polishing VFX effects and audio. Netflix recently revealed that 300 of its shows use generative AI. The integration is happening at a scale bigger than many viewers realize, Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck who covers the business of Hollywood, told WIRED earlier this month.

Since 2000, sex scenes in movies have declined by 40 percent, according to a 2023 study conducted by The Economist. But recent releases suggest that the industry may be turning a corner. “Movies are getting horny again,” one film critic who specializes in erotic thrillers told the BBC. According to a recent survey from entertainment research firm Luminate, despite an overall backlash against AI in Hollywood, one-third of consumers now feel indifferent toward the use of AI in production across all areas, except when it comes to writing and acting.

Rogue is making a bet that the continued adoption of AI tools—particularly ones focused on delivering premium visuals—could potentially supercharge that experience for viewers to the point where the quality of a performer’s delivery isn’t determined by whether it is AI or not, the cofounder says.

“We’re so used to uncensored meaning you get a fraction of the quality. Right now too much of the art form is being lost.”

The Best Budget Laptops to Get Your Money’s Worth

Wired August 17, 2026

HP (14-inch)

Amazon

Dell (8 GB)

Amazon (16-inch)

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Computers have put people on the moon. You'd think that given the miraculous technological utopia of our age, we’d also be able to get decently cheap laptops. For so long, that felt like a hopeless case. More recently, many budget laptops have become quite good. Chromebooks are more modern, and budget Windows laptops now offer strong battery life. There’s even a MacBook affordable enough to earn the “cheap” designation. If your budget for a computer is tight, I have you covered with my recommendations for the best affordable laptops.

For more laptop recommendations, be sure to check out our other computing guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Linux Laptops, Best Gaming Laptops, and Best MacBooks. Our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop can also help.

Updated August 2026: I've added the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 3, and MSI Cyborg A15. I’ve also confirmed accuracy and up-to-date pricing throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

HP

HP (14-inch)

Amazon (14-inch)

Thanks to Qualcomm's Snapdragon X chips, we finally have affordable Windows laptops that get great battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 14 is the best among those, so long as you can get it on discount. For starters, it has great specs, including 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. That screen, in particular, is a big deal for laptops at this price, as OLED displays offer such a massive step up from standard IPS displays. Its display isn't as sharp or bright as the MacBook Neo or Dell 14 Plus, though.

The HP OmniBook 5 is a highly portable little laptop, at just a half-inch thick. The touchpad is probably its biggest downside. Like many budget laptops, the touchpad feels sticky to use, making precise movements difficult. The keyboard is great, though, and the addition of a USB-A port is clutch.

There's a big caveat with the OmniBook 5's price. It retails for $1,300, but it’s often discounted at HP. com. I can typically find a configuration that sells for less than $700, sometimes as low as $550.

Apple

Amazon

Walmart

Apple

This one's easy. If you've always dreamed of owning a MacBook, but it was never in your price range, the MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is for you. It has plenty of shortcomings, mind you. Between the speed of USB-C ports and the lack of keyboard backlighting, Apple made lots of small compromises to get the price down to $699. Just 8 GB of RAM is the most serious detriment. You'll notice that every other laptop on this list starts at 16 GB, which has become the new standard. In my own testing, I was able to create a memory bottleneck without too much effort. But as a device for students, or just if you work at an office all day on a work computer and need something simple for weekends and evenings, the MacBook Neo’s performance should work well for you.

Its real strength is in its front-of-screen experience. It's the feeling you get every time you open the laptop, and that's where the MacBook Neo excels. A lot of that has to do with build quality and design, which are no less refined than the MacBooks that cost thousands more—with a dash of playfulness, thanks to the white keyboard and bolder colors. But the display is also worthy of recognition. It's both sharper and brighter than all its competitors, except for the Dell XPS 13.

Dell

Dell (8 GB)

Dell (16 GB)

I never thought a Windows laptop could pull off the trick of blending performance and affordability as well as the MacBook Neo, but the new Dell XPS 13 does it even better. The XPS 13 makes very few compromises, whether that's the portable design, the excellent display, the smooth trackpad, or the high speeds of the USB-C ports.

It has a couple of one-ups over the MacBook Neo, too. Some are quality-of-life improvements, like the backlit keyboard, the ability to charge from either side of the device, or the half-pound lighter weight. Other features are more substantial, such as the addition of a touchscreen and the 120-Hz refresh rate of the display. The 8 GB of RAM in the starting configuration is a severe limitation, but upgrading to the 16-GB model at $900 yields an incredible value. The 16-GB model is the one most people should buy, even if the $700 version with 8 GB is more tempting for budget-conscious buyers. Just be aware that 8 GB of memory in a modern Windows 11 laptop will start slowing down without too much effort.

HP

Amazon (16-inch)

Amazon (14-inch)

Walmart

The HP OmniBook 3 has the same performance, battery life, and OLED display as the OmniBook 5, but with a lower price. The OmniBook3 still comes with 16 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage (though you'll need to be mindful when you buy, as there are 8-GB models out there selling for the same price). When in doubt, HP. com tends to have the best deals on this laptop.

The most noticeable difference with the OmniBook 3 is that the quality of the chassis goes down; the 3’s thicker, plastic case feels much cheaper. There are smaller drawbacks as well, like the lack of a magnetic lid to securely close the laptop, the slower USB-A ports, and the really poor speakers. If those feel like minor nitpicks to you, saving the extra money on the OmniBook 3, rather than shelling out a bit more for the 5, is a smart move. The fact that you can get an OLED display and battery life this long-lasting on a device this cheap still blows me away.

MSI

Amazon (512 GB)

Best Buy (1 TB)

It's possible to buy a gaming laptop for less than $1,000, but right now, it's not recommended. There was a time when $700 gaming laptops were decent, but those days are long gone. The MSI Cyborg A15 with the RTX 5050 is the cheapest gaming laptop I've found that's actually worth buying. You still get the latest generation of Nvidia graphics, as well as a fast CPU from Intel. It’s not the prettiest laptop in the world, and it’s quite chunky, but it’s the best you’ll get for the price.

The Lenovo LOQ 15 with the RTX 5060 gets you a better screen (and better performance), but if you can't get your budget up to $1,300, go with the MSI Cyborg A15.

Asus

Amazon (8 GB)

If you want to find a laptop for around $300 or less, Chromebooks are still the way to go. Windows laptops at this price just aren't worth your time, due to the extreme performance compromises required to get the price down. The Acer Chromebook CX15, however, is the best ultra-cheap laptop I've used. Even with its bargain-basement price, this 15-inch Chromebook comes with 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. The 15-inch screen goes up to 300 nits of brightness, and even though the colors are a bit off, it has a 1080p resolution. The Intel Celeron CPU inside won't blow you away, but for the price, it certainly gets the job done.

There's also the Asus Chromebook CX14 (6/10, WIRED Recommends), a 14-inch version of this same laptop, which has a slightly sharper screen (due to the smaller display) and an overall more compact chassis. If you want to go even cheaper, there's a $199 version of this Chromebook with only 4 GB of RAM.

Framework

Framework

Most cheap laptops won't last you too long. They often function as a placeholder until you get something faster and more premium-feeling. Not so with the Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). Like other Framework computers, the Laptop 12 is completely upgradable, allowing you to access and swap out nearly every internal component. So long as Framework continues to hold up its end of the deal, you could hold onto it for years, upgrading it through many generations of CPUs. What’s amazing is how easy Framework has made installing components and upgrading them yourself—it’s possible to do in minutes.

The DIY Edition, which doesn't come with RAM and storage, starts at just $549. While the performance and display aren't exactly premium, I was surprised by how high-end the touchpad and keyboard feel. If you want something affordable (and highly customizable) that you want to last more than a few years, this is it.

Here at WIRED, we never recommend products we haven't tested ourselves—and I’ve tried hundreds of laptops over the years. I left many laptops off this list due to price, quality, or both. While I stand by my top-pick recommendations above, there are a few additional laptops I've tested that are still worth buying for a particular use case.

Lenovo LOQ 15 for $1,400: This fantastic gaming laptop used to sell for $900, despite coming with an RTX 5060. And unlike so many other affordable gaming laptops, this one comes with a solid IPS panel that has not only a fast refresh rate but also great image quality. So no, it's not extremely cheap, but it's worth considering because it remains the best value in gaming laptops right now.

Acer Chromebook Plus 516 for $479: Chromebooks are really at their best when they cost less than $500. They thrive as cheap laptops that don't feel cheap. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has one primary advantage over other laptops around this price: its touchpad. I care a lot about touchpad quality, as it's an area where budget laptops tend to make compromises despite being a component that can impact day-to-day laptop use. Poor touchpad quality can make simple things like drag-and-drop or text selection frustrating. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has a really nice touchpad with a smooth surface for your finger to swipe or drag across. It makes a huge difference.

Acer Nitro V 16 for $900: No gaming laptop selling for this price is going to be perfect. Far from it. The Acer Nitro V 16 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) has a big compromise that I need to warn you about up front: its 135-watt power adapter. It's just not enough to keep the Nitro V 16 fully powered during many of the GPU-heavy games I tested, such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong. That means even if the laptop is plugged in, it'll start to drain the battery when you tax the GPU hard enough. That sounds awful, and it is. Acer could have easily sold the Nitro V 16 with a larger adapter. But the battery only drains in certain games and only when playing in Turbo or Performance modes. Stick to Balanced mode, and you'll be fine, as it only drops performance by around 5 percent. All said, I still think the MSI Cyborg A15 is the better laptop for this reason.

Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $379: Lenovo’s Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) quickly became one of my favorite gadgets of 2024, despite its small size. That’s the whole point of this 11-inch detachable laptop, which is incredibly fun to use around the house and throw in a bag when it’s time to go. The keyboard detaches from the screen, so it makes for a nice tablet when paired with ChromeOS's Android apps. With the keyboard attached, you can get some work done. At nearly 10 hours on average, its battery life will easily get you through the day, too.

Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1.

Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1: 16-inch laptops tend to be more expensive than smaller options, making them hard to find at a cheap price. The Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) is a 16-inch laptop that tried to squeeze out just enough quality to make it worth the price. While the display has typical deficiencies (such as poor color coverage), I do appreciate that it doesn't have a matte finish, which brings out more clarity in the panel. I also found the keyboard tiresome to type on, and ultimately feel the OmniBook 3 is the better laptop for the price.

Asus Vivobook 14: As one of the first cheap laptops to use the Snapdragon X, I praised this laptop through 2025 for its excellent battery life. But once the OmniBook 5 and OmniBook 3 came along, I stopped recommending the Vivobook 14. That's primarily because of how much better the OLED screens are on the OmniBook devices compared to the washed-out display that comes on the Vivobook 14. But if you ever see this drop to below the price of the OmniBook 3 and want the cheapest Windows laptop possible, it might be worth considering.

What Are Important Specs in a Cheap Laptop?

Read our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop if you want all the details on specs and what to look for. In short, your budget is the most important factor, as it determines what you can expect out of the device you're purchasing. Next, you should consider display size, chassis thickness, CPU, memory, storage, and port selection. While appropriate specs can vary wildly when you're considering laptops ranging from $200 to around $1,000, there are a few hard lines I don't recommend crossing.

For example, don't buy a laptop if it doesn't have a display resolution of at least 1920 x 1080. In 2025, there's just no excuse for anything less than that. You should also never buy a laptop without at least 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. Even in Chromebooks, these specs are becoming the new standard. You're selling yourself short by getting anything less. Another rule is to avoid a Windows laptop with an Intel Celeron processor—leave those for Chromebooks only.

Specs are only half the battle, though. Based on our years of testing, laptop manufacturers tend to make compromises in display quality and touchpad quality. You can't tell from the photos or listed specs online, but once you get the laptop in your hands, you may notice that the colors of the screen look a bit off or that the touchpad feels choppy to use. It's nearly impossible to find laptops under $500 that don't compromise in these areas, but this is where our reviewers and testers can help.

How Much RAM Do You Need in a Cheap Laptop?

The simple answer? You need at least 8 GB of RAM, but you'll likely want at least 16 GB. These days, lots of Windows laptops that fall into the “budget” category come with 16 GB of RAM standard t, as part of the Copilot+ PC marketing push. That's a great value that ensures you'll get the best performance out of your laptop, especially when running heavier applications or multitasking. Either way, it's important to factor in the price of the RAM because manufacturers will often charge $100 or even $200 to double the memory.

On Chromebooks, there are some rare occasions where 4 GB of RAM is acceptable, but only on the very cheapest models that are less than $200. Even budget Chromebooks like the Asus Chromebook CX15 now start with 8 GB of RAM.

Prices are constantly shifting, however, largely because of the ongoing memory shortage. We are starting to see the return of 8 GB in laptops like the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13, but I recommend opting for 16 GB if at all possible.

Are There Any Good Laptops Under $300?

Yes, but you need to be careful. Don't just go buy a random laptop on Amazon for less than $300, as you'll likely end up with an outdated, slow device you'll regret having purchased. You might be tempted by something like this or this, but trust me—there are better options, some of which you'll find in this guide.

For starters, you shouldn't buy a Windows laptop for less than $300. That price puts you solidly in cheap Chromebook territory. These Chromebooks are budget-level in terms of quality, but they're still better in almost every way than their Windows counterparts of a similar price. A good example is the Asus Chromebook CX15.

If you want a Windows laptop that won't give you instant buyer's remorse, you'll need to spend at least a few hundred more. Once you hit $500 or $600, there are some more solid Windows laptops available, such as the HP OmniBook 3. Even in that case, though, you're making some compromises in features like touchpad quality and chassis thickness. But as a general principle, Windows laptops only start to become worth buying in the $500-plus range.

Should You Get a Cheap Windows Laptop or Chromebook?

The eternal question. If you're looking for a laptop for less than $500, I highly recommend that you opt for a Chromebook. I know that won't be a possibility for everyone, as some people require certain applications that require a Windows laptop or a MacBook. If you do decide to get a Chromebook, make sure all of your connected accessories and other devices are compatible.

Chromebooks give you access to a full desktop Chrome browser, as well as Android apps. While that leaves some gaps for apps that some may need, you might be surprised by how much you can get done without the need to install any software. Most applications have web versions that are every bit as useful.

While Chromebooks are most well-known as junky student laptops, the “Chromebook Plus” designation has filled in the gap between dirt-cheap Chromebooks and $800 Windows laptops. You'll find some great Chromebook Plus options in the $400 to $600 range that have better performance and displays and look a bit more like a modern laptop. The Acer Chromebook Plus 514 is a great example of this. You can read more about the differences between Windows laptops and Chromebooks here.

Review (2026): CookUnity Prepared Delivery Meals

Wired August 17, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

9/10

My lunch felt impossible. Was my fried chicken actually … crispy and moist?

This result was by no means likely. After all, I'd received this chicken in a sealed microwavable tray three days ago, by courier from Seattle to Portland, Oregon. It seemed unlikely that my Night Market Chicken from meal delivery service CookUnity would stand up to the harsh light of day when reheated.

And yet, here we were. When heated in an air fryer, the chicken's breading was nicely crisp. The meat was tender, juicy even. The Asian-influenced sesame-soy glaze was pleasantly sweet and tangy, paired with a heaping portion of egg fried rice. If this had been takeout food from a restaurant down the street, I would have accepted it gladly.

CookUnity’s Night Market Chicken, from chef Kevin Meehan

CookUnity Prepared Meals

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

In fact, a number of the meals I've tasted from CookUnity over the past two years have rivaled restaurant takeout—a genuine rarity among prepared delivery meals. Most of the big meal delivery services have branched out into ready-to-heat prepared meals, and I've tried most of them. CookUnity is the best I've tried by a pretty long margin, while maintaining similar prices: $12 to $13 a meal on the most common plans.

CookUnity stands out for two reasons. One is that it's less reliant on the microwave—offering alternate instructions that still usually only take five or 10 minutes. The other is that the meals are prepared in kitchens run by actual restaurant chefs, who each put their name and face on the box.

My tasty Night Market Chicken came from the Seattle commissary of Michelin-decorated LA chef Kevin Meehan. And while I doubt Michelin will come calling this time, it was a genuine prize winner among work lunches hoovered over my laptop. And while last year I worried that veggies were a rarity, this year CookUnity's meals have expanded in both quantity and variety.

Here's how it works, and my (quite good) results.

The reason CookUnity is not like other prepared meal services is that, quite frankly, it's not like other prepared meal services. CookUnity is a singular model, something like a cross between a meal service and DoorDash.

CookUnity Prepared Meals

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Rather than make recipes in a top-down corporate kitchen, CookUnity is regional. The service enlists local and national chefs and promises to bring restaurant-quality meals to the home—prepared according to recipes from occasionally quite big names. (Hello, Jose Garces. Hello, Esther Choi.)

Like a lot of meal kits, CookUnity is a subscription service. You choose the number of prepared meals that you want delivered each week—and then pick out your meals from that week's menu. It's around $12 a meal if you get 10 portions a week—or more than $15 if you only want four meals. This is more than scratch cooking or a frozen dinner, but less than restaurant delivery or takeout.

The meal service is run out of eight regional commissary hubs around the United States and Canada: Seattle, LA, Austin, Chicago, New York, Atlanta, Miami, and Toronto. Each hub has its own stable of chefs: Some are local. Some are kitchens operated by national chefs. This does have the side effect of leaving out most of West Virginia and a good swath of the Plains states.

If your zip code is covered, it goes like this: You sign up for a certain number of single-serve meals per week, which arrive in heatable trays in a big, cold-packed box. A representative menu for each region is available here, but you won't see any given week's menu where you live till you've entered your zip code and handed out your email address. (I know, I don't love this either.)

Generally, if you order by Thursday, you can have delivery of your week's meals by Monday. Meals can be filtered for meal type (salad, meats and twos, pasta, et al.), vegan, vegetarian, GLP-1, fiber-rich, precise calorie counts (whether high or low), and a whole host of allergens. They can also be sorted by chef, and range from dainty 500-calorie lunches to 1,200-calorie feasts like that Night Market Chicken.

CookUnity Prepared Meals

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Each meal arrives in a tray that looks like a TV dinner, and I can microwave it in three minutes if I want. I usually don't, because each meal also has “chef-recommended” heating methods for optimal results. Maybe this involves a 10-minute turn in a toaster oven or a five-minute sauté. (Often, I sub in an air fryer where toaster ovens are suggested, with excellent results.)

CookUnity Farro, Beets & Greens Salad from chef Dustin Taylor

One of the most interesting things about CookUnity is that chefs and menus are different for each region. My hub, in Seattle, is among the smallest with only a dozen chefs. But because each chef offers anywhere from eight to 20 meals, my weekly menu in Seattle still ranged above 200 dishes. This is a far greater variety than when I first tried the service last year.

CookUnity calls itself a “chef collective.” In practice, this means it enlists restaurant chefs, including an interesting preponderance of Iron Chef alumni, to design recipes and run teams of cooks in any of the eight regional commissary kitchens. Ingredients are sourced for the chefs by CookUnity in a shared kitchen. CookUnity handles the delivery. It also handles the packaging technology, which, through the magic of modified atmosphere packaging, can be stored at fridge temps for four to seven days.

Many chefs expand nationally to multiple hubs. In Seattle, I can order sweet-sauced barbecue chicken herbed up with Haitian epis from Texas West-Indian chef Nahika Hillery, chicken adobo from Los Angeles chef Stacy Baraeng, or a summery udon from Esther Choi.

But my favorite dishes didn't come from the national chefs and celebrities—and indeed, the meat in a pork adobo from Baraeng came out a bit tough. What I loved best were the flavorful Indian gravies from Odisha-born Seattle chef Gaurav Raj, whether a lightly fiery chicken lababdar or a smooth and rich butter chicken.

CookUnity Prepared Meals

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

At a lower cost, each of Raj's delivery meals consistently tastes better than the (admittedly not great) Punjabi restaurant down the street from me—less sugary, more rich, with saffron-tinged basmati and chicken that remains juicy and plump, not overcooked. Raj's Indian gravies offer the most compelling argument for me to order CookUnity, in a city (Portland) where the best Indian food is often a half-hour drive into the suburbs.

But, of course, Raj's meals are available only to those served by the Seattle hub. Others, near Los Angeles or Atlanta, may have other local chefs who offer similarly compelling arguments. I wouldn't know.

CookUnity Beef Stroganoff with Truffle & Pappardelle from chef John DeLucie

The strength of CookUnity is that each regional hub is basically local. But this is also a potential weakness: Each regional hub is different. Each hub has greater or lesser variety. Each also has a different selection of chefs and meals.

But my good experience with the Seattle hub might translate to what you'll find in a different kitchen, with different cooks. This may be true even if the same chef's name and face are on your meal box. Some chefs operate four or five kitchens at different hubs, and different kitchens may have different results, even with the same recipes. And heck, I've had different results even from the same chefs. I can only speak to my own good experience and the good experience of my colleague Louryn Strampe, who ordered out of the Chicago hub.

Note that while CookUnity offers a much bigger caloric range than most prepared meal kits, usually the big feasts are heavily carb-loaded: rice, noodles, pasta. Those looking for a focus on proteins and veggies can find them easily, but usually in more moderate portions. Food cost is food cost. Starches are cheap.

But I have reason to believe that CookUnity's other hubs also offer good cooking—and that has a lot to do with CookUnity's business model. The overall factor that I think makes CookUnity work is healthy competition.

Each CookUnity chef making prepared meals is, essentially, a competing food business within the same big commissary kitchen. Their name is on each box, and a good number of the chefs have restaurants and reputations to protect. There are many incentives to make each meal interesting and delicious. My experience bears this out.

Review: Skylight Buddy

Wired August 17, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

Like many 4-year-olds, my son is stubborn. He'll do his best to distract and resist basic activities, like getting in the bath, brushing his teeth, and lying down for bed. The Skylight Buddy—the new kids’ device from the makers of the popular digital calendar—promised to engage him and keep him on a schedule without me needing to nag.

I was dubious that the Skylight Buddy could make good on its claims. The device is designed for kids 4 to 10, and because my son only recently turned 4, I figured he'd probably still be a little young for it. Also, regardless of age, empowering little kids to autonomously stick to their routines and chores is a tall order. However, after almost two weeks of testing, my son has been so excited to use this device and complete the tasks it shows him.

The Skylight Buddy works by reminding my son of his morning and evening routines, like brushing his teeth. It uses both words and picture icons, which is crucial because he can't read yet. Now, his favorite part of the day is when the device congratulates him on his completed tasks at bedtime. While some features are paywalled, you don’t absolutely have to subscribe for your kids to enjoy the Skylight Buddy. Plus, there's no microphone or camera in the device, making it a safe addition for a kid's bedroom. It also works seamlessly with Skylight's digital calendars if you happen to already use one in your home.

The Skylight Buddy sits at just under 7.5 inches tall, with a 1024 x 600 resolution touchscreen. It has a big, yellow half-circle “select” button and volume controls on the top. There are two speakers (one on each side of the device), and the bottom base doubles as a dim night-light. The only other included piece is a power cord that isn't particularly long, so you'll need to place it on a tabletop near an outlet in your child's room. You can also add on a silicone case ($20) if you're worried about your kid knocking it off the table (or you want to give it a pop of color, as the cover comes in purple, green, and blue, while the device itself only comes in white).

Skylight Buddy

Rating: 8/10

For setup, you’ll use the Skylight app, which is the same one you'd use if you have Skylight's digital calendars or photo frames. The Buddy has its own section of the app, separate from the calendar. But because I also use the calendar, my son’s tasks from the Buddy appear in both the general Skylight menus and the specific Buddy menu. Every to-do I've created for my son lives in the Tasks section, and when I created each item, the app had me choose whether the task in question was a chore or routine. Chores have many details you can fill in; you can also mark them as up for grabs if you’re happy for any family member to complete them. Routines let you choose how often a specific routine should repeat and what time of day it should happen.

I focused on routines for my 4-year-old, since I’m not ready to track chores for him. He likes to help flip the laundry loads and “wash” the dishes (mainly spray them with water, but he does get most of the food off!), though for now, I’m more interested in him building consistent habits. The routines I created pop up on the screen under “Morning” and “Evening,” but there’s also an “Afternoon” option for routines you assign for that time of day.

The Buddy also has sound machine and wake-up features, plus a little night-light at the bottom of the device. You'll set this up in the app under the Sleep & Wake menu, which lets you add sleep sounds and a night-light for bedtime, along with a morning alarm. I tried these features, but they’re not ultimately going to replace the Hatch Baby in my son’s routine. The Buddy’s sound options are more limited and not as nice as the music from the Hatch Baby. And not only is the night-light dim, but my son looks forward to his Hatch turning green when it's time for him to wake up. Still, the Buddy has a nice set of options if you need a sound machine or an alarm clock for your kiddo.

I didn't think my son would particularly care about this device, but the second we unboxed it, he wanted to use it. He immediately started pushing buttons and trying to scroll around on the screen. The first night after I set it up, I explained the tasks and what each on-screen icon meant, and he actually ran to brush his teeth so he could check it off.
